This gives us 2^{50+25+12+6+3+1}=2^{97} So 100! is actually divisible by 2^{97} , and besides that it’s also obviously divisible by 11,13,17 and 19 whose product is more than 10000 , so it must be way larger than 2^{97}\cdot 10000 which is way more than 2^{97}\cdot 2^{10} . So, all told, 2^{100!} is much, much larger than \left(2^{100}\right)! .
what-real-numbers-will-we-never-know-eve: What real numbers will we never know (even the approximate) value of? — \tan\left(9^{9^{9^9}}\right) . I contend that we won’t ever know whether this number is positive or negative, whether it is more than a billion or less than a billionth, whether its integer value is odd or even, anything of the sort. It’s a well-defined real number, but to determine any of those things you will likely need to spend more than the energy resources of the entire universe. (EDIT: To clarify, there are certainly things we know about this number - for example, it is a real number, rather than undefined; it is irrational, and in fact transcendental. I’m specifically answering the question about knowing its ”approximate value”. We can’t place this number in any reasonable interval. Also to clarify, this is the standard \tan function, whose input is expressed in radians). It is possible, of course, that there’s some insane shortcut, but I wouldn’t expect there to be. You can easily make up such numbers. This particular one is based on the fact that \tan(x) is very sensitive to the precise value of x \bmod \pi , which means you have to fit in exactly as many \pi 's as possible in 9^{9^{9^9}} and know what’s left over with some reasonable precision. That’s unlikely to ever be feasible, and if by some wild miracle it does become feasible, just add one more 9 to the power tower. Oh, for those of you who are rushing over to Wolfram|Alpha to try this out: let me save you the trouble. But again, you can concoct any number of such expressions, for whatever that’s worth.
what-are-coffin-problems-in-mathematics: What are coffin problems in mathematics? — “Coffin problems” are extremely difficult math problems which, nevertheless, have elementary solutions. They were devised for and used by admission committees at Soviet universities in the 70’s and 80’s to keep Jewish candidates (and other “undesirables”) out of the most prestigious universities, such as Moscow State. Only undesirable candidates were asked these questions in the oral entrance exams . For more on the history of the practice, see: Chapter 3 of Edward Frenkel’s “ Love and Math ”, or Frenkel’s article “ The Fifth Problem: Math and anti-Semitism in the Soviet Union ”. Alexander Shen’s “ Entrance Examinations to the Mekh-Mat ”, The Mathematical Intelligencer Vol. 16, No. 4, 1994. Tanya Khovanova’s “ Coffins ” page, and her article " Killer Problems " in The American Mathematical Monthly, Vol. 119, No. 10 (2012), pp. 815-82. Articles by Mark and Anatoly Vershik . Another reference suggested by Ted Alper is the book “ You Failed your Math Test, Comrade Einstein ” by M. Shifman. The articles by Shen and Khovanova, and the solution set by Ilan Vardi , contain a large collection of Coffin problems. Some of these problems have also appeared elsewhere, for example in Peter Winkler’s wonderful collection or in various math olympiads. The tragedy of these problems is that, despite their ignominious origin, many of them are absolute gems, a testimony to the ingenuity and creativity of those tasked with finding problems that are impossible to solve in the setting of an oral exam, while being “defensible” in the sense that short, ingenious, elementary solutions do exist. In my mind, one of the best of these problems is the following geometry pearl, which is also the one in Winkler’s book (p. 47, “Sphere and Quadrilateral”): A quadrilateral in space has all of its edges tangent to a sphere. Prove that the points of tangency are coplanar. (A quadrilateral in space is simply four points A,B,C,D and four straight line segments AB,BC,CD,DA . The four points may or may not lie on a plane.) Approaching this problem in any of the usual or not-quite-usual ways – with analytic geometry in space, or vector calculus, or complex coordinates on the Riemann sphere – is extremely difficult. However, an ingenious trick allows for a solution in a few lines. Each vertex of the quadrilateral has two edges emanating from it and tangent to the sphere at two points; the distances d from the vertex to these two points are the same (why?). Put a mass of 1/d at that vertex. For any two vertices, their center of mass is now precisely the point of tangency between them (observe how this doesn’t work with mass of d : you need a small mass for the larger distance!). Therefore, the center of mass of the entire contraption lies at a point which also lies on lines connecting opposite pairs of tangency points, which means the whole thing is in one plane. \blacksquare Ilan Vardi presents here several alternate solutions, including an algebraic one spanning four pages of calculations. This is not an easy problem by any stretch of the imagination, and the fact that it nevertheless has such a short solution is truly miraculous.
what-is-a-simple-explanation-for-the-gen: What is a simple explanation for the general equation of the second degree? — - Can you solve x^2=9 ? - Yes: x=3 . - There's another solution. - Oh yeah, x=-3 works as well. - Good. How about (x+1)^2=9 ? - Well, I know that (x+1)^2=x^2+2x+ ... - Stop! Resist the reflex to expand this. It's easier if you don't. - But how can I solve (x+1)^2=9 without expanding the square? - You've already solved a very similar equation just a moment ago. - But turning x into x+1 changes everything. - There's another way to look at it: give x+1 a new name, like u . - Ok, how does that help? - What is the equation now? - It's u^2=9 . But that's cheating! - No, you've done nothing wrong. What is u ? - It is either 3 or -3. - Right. So what is x ? - Well u=x+1 , so x is either 2 or -4. - Brilliant. You just solved x^2+2x+1=9 by looking at it in a different way! - Yeah, well, but you made it up so it works nicely. What if it didn't? - What general family of equations do you think you can solve now? - Um, stuff like (x+\mbox{blah})^2=\mbox{whatever} . I just give x+\mbox{blah} a new name, solve, and recover x . - Exactly. And guess what? This is enough to solve any second-degree equation. - Huh? - Suppose I give you x^2+10x = 11 . What would you do? - I've no idea. It doesn't look at all like (x+\mbox{blah})^2=\mbox{anything} . - Don't be so pessimistic. Do you see that \mbox{blah}=5 almost works? - How "almost"? Why 5? - Try it. - Well (x+5)^2 = x^2+10x+25 . But that's not what's in the equation. - What is? - Just x^2+10x . - ...which you now know is (x+5)^2-25 . - Oh. Right. So the equation is (x+5)^2-25=11 . - ...which is... - (x+5)^2 = 36 . - ...so... - I rename x+5 to u (it still feels like cheating), get u^2=36 , so u is 6 or -6 and x is 1 or -11. That's it? - Yes. What sort of equations can you solve now? - Well, it looks like I can handle x^2+\mbox{something}\,\, x = \mbox{whatever} , provided \mbox{something} is even. - Why do you need \mbox{something} to be even? - Because what you did there was take that \mbox{something} , which was 10, and take half of it to be the \mbox{blah} . - That's right. So you can't take half of 7? - I can, but it's a fraction. - So? - I hate fractions. - LOL, ok. But they work just the same. - Fine. So I can handle x^2+\mbox{something}\,\, x = \mbox{whatever} . I take half of the \mbox{something} , call it \mbox{blah} , find the correction so I can write (x+\mbox{blah})^2-\mbox{correction} = \mbox{whatever} , move the numbers together, rename x+\mbox{blah} to u , and solve. - Excellent. Can you do what you just said with letters instead of blahs and whatevers? - I think so: x^2+2bx=c (x+b)^2-b^2=c (x+b)^2 = c+b^2 x+b = \pm \sqrt{c+b^2} x = -b \pm \sqrt{c+b^2} . - Excellent. We usually write a quadratic as ax^2+bx+c=0 , but you can just divide through by a and move the constant to the other side to get exactly what you just solved. You're done!
was-what-the-mathematician-ed-witten-did: Was what the mathematician Ed Witten did to receive the Fields medal legitimate mathematics, or not? — “Physicists on Quora and in the physics community claim that Witten does not follow mathematical rules in his creation of string theory. So was his mathematics for the fields medal legitimate or is it possibly nonsense?” (From the question’s details.) The Fields Medal Let me tell you something about the Fields medal. Apart from the fact that it is the most prestigious award in the mathematical world (so you may safely assume it does not get awarded to anyone for any kind of “arbitrary nonsense”), there's another aspect of the medal that's somewhat less well known. The Fields medal is only awarded to people under 40. This is why Andrew Wiles, who sensationally proved Fermat’s Last Theorem, wasn't awarded one. So weren't many other incredible mathematicians who missed the deadline, so to speak. The reason this age limit is in place is because the medal was meant to encourage young researchers. It was not designed as a “lifetime achievement” medal, like the Nobel Prize, but as a way to support or motivate promising mathematicians so they keep on researching and producing revolutionary ideas. Not entirely surprisingly, this ideal doesn't always play out. Creating truly novel, groundbreaking theories isn't something many people can do once in a lifetime, let alone twice. Since the Fields medal is so prestigious, and is awarded to so few people, it is naturally awarded to mathematicians who have already produced the finest of the finest in original research, and it's almost unreasonable to expect them to continue to be as sensationally creative. Indeed, for a good number of past medalists, nothing they did after the medal comes close to the body of work that won them the Fields. To be clear, this isn't any kind of criticism or a downplaying of their ingenuity: every single Fields medalist did something incredible. It's just that the “young, promising researcher” thing is setting the bar quite unreasonably high. There are, however, exceptions. A number of awardees were such profoundly transformative mathematicians that they achieved no less after the medal than before it – so much so that they perhaps would have been awarded a Fields for their latter work alone. I'm far from qualified to judge who, exactly, deserves to be on the shortlist of the shortlist, the elite of the peak of human mathematical achievement. Grothendieck is certainly among them. So is Serre, and Atle Selberg who developed the profound Trace Formula that bears his name six years after receiving the medal, and several others I would dare name. And, in my mind, for whatever that's worth, so is Witten. Witten’s Work Ed Witten was awarded the Fields medal for a series of groundbreaking mathematical discoveries which, in the words of Sir Michael Atiyah, have “made a profound impact on contemporary mathematics.” Through Witten’s work, Atiyah continued, “physics is once again providing a rich source of inspiration and insight in mathematics.” Witten was awarded the medal in 1990, when he was 39 years old (as you can imagine, it's quite uncommon for people to land it long before the age 40 limit). By then he created topological quantum field theory and discovered deep links between Morse theory and supersymmetry. Let's be clear: those are mathematical achievements. The IMU didn't just decide it was time to give some physicist a medal. The mathematical theory of knots and 3-manifolds, to give one example, is forever changed thanks to Witten’s pre-Fields work. But he wasn't quite done yet. The “second revolution” of string theory was sparked in 1995 by Witten’s amazing discovery that the various extant string theories are but shadows of a single idea now called an M-theory. That's physics, so to speak. But in math, the Seiberg-Witten invariants had an impact on the theory of 4-manifolds that's at least as profound as his earlier work on 3-manifolds, and I've seen mathematicians refer to them as Witten’s finest achievement. This is 1994, four years after the mathematical world already deemed his work worthy of its highest honor. Putting in question the legitimacy of Witten’s contributions to mathematics is a few notches beyond ridiculous. He stands out even among the best of the best of them, as one of the few who continued to work miracles even after they received the medal. String Theory The question refers to “string theory arbitrary nonsense”, so I feel obliged to say something about that as well. String Theory isn't complete or perfect, and may never become either. It may eventually come to be understood as merely a step, or more likely a collection of important steps and some missteps that were still inevitable in our quest for a unified theory. But branding it “nonsense” is just ignorant. Whatever it is – almost the whole truth, a glimpse of the truth, or a beautiful non-truth which miraculously manages to come ever so close to the truth – one thing it cannot be is nonsense. It's a magnificent, shining edifice of such internal cohesiveness and beauty that it almost doesn't matter if it doesn't describe our own universe: the universe it does describe deserves our attention and exploration. Like many theories under formation, it has parts that are conjectural or speculative, but it also has huge sections that are worked out in complete rigor. Like many present and future physical theories, it makes predictions that are difficult to confirm with available technology. That doesn't mean it's “not falsifiable” in principle. In fact, any new mathematical theory that produces the same results as QED or QCD is by definition falsifiable: it would have been falsified by any experiment that would refute QED or QCD. There's huge value in finding new mathematical frameworks that “merely” recast the current theories in a new setting. This isn't a retraction of Popper’s ideas about science; it's the observation that multiple distinct theories can produce the same observables and are therefore worthy of equal scrutiny. It's been said that string theory already made one profound prediction: it predicts gravity. This is, of course, a joke, but it has a kernel of truth. A theory that reproduces the standard model of particle physics and yields gravity as a natural outcome does something very special that the current standard model doesn't do. It could be wrong, but it cannot be worthless. Mathematical Rigor Finally, I believe that there's enormous misconception around the “non-rigorous” aspects of Witten’s work (as well as others, such as Thurston's), and around the whole notion of mathematical discovery, conjecture and proof. Intuitive ideas, half-formed theories, heuristic arguments, nonsensical transformations, provably false derivations, partial analogies, guesses, wishes, and vaguely describable dreams are a huge, crucial and inevitable part of mathematics. Missing this is misunderstanding mathematics and creativity. Proofs don't emerge in a vacuum. Theorems don't fall like ripe apples on mathematicians’ heads out of some divine tree. Everything comes from imagination, and while we are imagining and fantasizing we are often deliberately and knowingly making non-rigorous statements. Doing mathematics any other way is like programming a MacBook to spit out true statements in ZFC. Rigorous and correct, but pointless. Criticizing Witten’s work for being non-rigorous is making two profound errors. First, a tremendous amount of his work is completely rigorous. Second, the parts that aren't matter just as much. They point the way for others to fill the gaps and formalize the arguments. They create spaces for people to work in. They guide and innovate in original, imaginative ways. Asking good questions and making good conjectures has the same amount of value to mathematical development, or more, as proving things. Anyone who told you otherwise misunderstands what it means to do mathematics and to be a mathematician. This came out longer than I had expected, but honestly it's even less emotional than it would have been had I written it immediately when the question was asked. I feel strongly about these things, yes. And I hope I've answered your question.
what-is-a-great-riddle-that-has-no-right: What is a great riddle that has no right answer? — A group of people are standing around in a circle. Every ten seconds, every person simultaneously shoots a random other person (with a laser tag system, of course. Nobody is actually hurt). If you're hit, you're out. Everyone is a great shot: they don't miss. Whoever they picked at random to take out is out. Ten seconds later, once again, everyone still standing shoots someone else at random. And so it goes on until one of two things happen: either there's a last lucky person standing, or there's nobody left. Question : what's the probability that nobody's left at the end of the game? The answer obviously depends on the number of people we had to begin with. The probability is one thing if you start with 5 people, and another thing if you start with 50. So, being the mathematicians that we are, we're curious about the value of this probability when the initial number of people is really large – a million, a billion, etc. "As n tends to infinity", to use the common math parlance. So, what is it? What is this limiting value of that probability? Does it tend to zero? Does it tend to 100%? Does it tend to some value in between? The actual answer to the question as I phrased it is that there is no answer . The probability, as a function of the number of people n , does not tend to any limit . It fluctuates, without converging. The answer to such questions is very often 0 or 1 ( Zero–one law ), and sometimes it's some limiting intermediate value which we may or may not be able to calculate explicitly, but it's really rare to have such naturally-defined probabilities that fluctuate for no obvious reason (it's easy to make it so that the values depend on the parity of n , for example, and then it's no surprise that they don't converge. But this isn't the case here). Here's a graph of the probability p that nobody survives, as a function of \log(n) . This is taken from the paper " The asymptotics of group Russian roulette " by van de Brug, Kager and Meester.
what-is-the-point-of-pure-mathematics: What is the point of pure mathematics? — …are there any realistic benefits that actually help the world run? (Original question details) How is "actually helping the world run" synonymous with "having a point"? Does music help the world run? Cosmology? Cricket? Sculpture? Ballet? Philosophy? 3D Animation? Archaeology? Caber tossing? Mathematics is a huge edifice of human thought, more beautiful and deep than anything else for those with the training and inclination to appreciate it. That is point enough. That's not to say that pure mathematics doesn't also have practical applications - the point is that it doesn't need those in order to matter. But of course, it does have such applications. Time and time again we've learned that mathematical abstractions find unexpected applications, and are in fact completely necessary for us to understand the world around us, and to influence it. Modern theories of physics - general relativity, quantum field theories, string theory - rely on very deep and abstract mathematical ideas. The study of algorithms and data structures, forming the foundation of computer science, requires a healthy dose of "pure math", and many extremely mundane technologies utilize those ideas (an often-quoted example is Google's original PageRank algorithm, which is an instance of an idea from graph theory). It is hard to imagine modern Economics or Earth sciences without statistics, another field that relies heavily on pure mathematics. However, as I said, most mathematicians - even those working in combinatorics, statistics or theoretical computer science, fields that are very close to engineering - don't need those applications in order to enjoy their work, or justify it. In fact, some of them positively relish the fact that they operate in purely abstract serenity, untainted, as it were, by machineries and technologies and so-called "applications". Hardy famously expressed this view in A Mathematician's Apology . Caring about why every natural number is the sum of four squares requires nothing more than intellectual curiosity, and satisfying our desire to pursue such questions in the name of sheer curiosity is the "point" of pure mathematics. (This image shows the distribution of the roots of a certain family of polynomials, discussed here ).
how-do-you-prove-that-lim-limits-n-to-in: How do you prove that \lim_\limits{n\to\infty}e^{-n}\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{n^k}{k!}=\frac{1}{2}? — Oh man, you totally spoiled it! This isn’t how you ask the question, come on ! You ask it like this: What is \displaystyle \lim_{n\to\infty} e^{-n}\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{n^k}{k!} \,\,\text{ ?} And then you sit back and enjoy the spectacle of everyone saying that it’s obviously 1 , and they explain why, and it’s so clear that it doesn’t even require proof but you ask them to prove it anyway, and they try, and they fail (or worse: succeed), and you ask them if they still think it’s 1 , and they say yeah but some of the confidence is gone, and you play them for just as long as it pleases you until you inform them they are exactly 100% off. So, why does everyone think this limit equals 1 , and why is that not true, and why is it actually \frac{1}{2} ? Well, for n very large, the sum \sum_{k=0}^n \frac{n^k}{k!} is about e^n . Right? It’s just the Taylor series of the exponential function. So then we multiply that by e^{-n} and get just about 1 , and as we let n grow this just becomes more and more accurate, so the limit has to be simply 1 . I mean it has to. Right? Wrong. So what’s wrong here? Well, you may feel a little uncomfortable about that Taylor business. I mean, sure, the sum \displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^n \frac{x^k}{k!} Is a partial sum of the Taylor series of e^x , so its limit for fixed x as n\to\infty is indeed e^x . But here we are doing something a little suspicious: we’re asking n to perform double duty as both the summation range and the variable of the power series. One thing, at any rate, should be clear: the statement \displaystyle e^n=?=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{n^k}{k!} makes no sense at all. The variable n is free on the left side and bound on the right. Ok. So that naive interpretation is out the window. How do we evaluate that limit? There’s a beautiful, masterful way to solve this that’s almost sleight of hand. It goes like this: this is precisely the limiting probability of a random Poisson variable with parameter \lambda=n to be less than its expectation. Such a variable is distributed just like the sum of n independent Poisson variables with parameter \lambda=1 , and such a sum (normalized by its variance, \sqrt{n} , which doesn’t matter here) converges in distribution to a normal distribution. What’s the probability that a normal random variable be less than its mean? Why it’s \frac{1}{2} , of course. Done. QED. Wait, what? Yes, really. If you know about the Central Limit Theorem, this is exactly what it says if you take random variables X_1,X_2,\ldots each of which is Poisson(1). Good, routine exercise in applying CLT to random Poisson variables. But what if you don’t know about the CLT or it just didn’t occur to you to interpret this limit as a probability? Then this is, honestly, quite a hard problem. The CLT is a powerful theorem which hides quite a bit of theory, offering it virtually for free. Without it, you’re on your own here, and I don’t know a really easy way to prove this. Some clever integral manipulations and transformations are needed.
is-a-b-1-1-the-only-solution-of-the-equa: Is (a,b)=(1,1) the only solution of the equation 3^a = b^2+2  where a,b are integers? — Alright, buckle up. I'm going use this little problem as an excuse to introduce the wonders of Algebraic Number Theory, at least a small portion of it. Ready? Ok. We're trying to solve 3^n = m^2+2 where m,n are positive integers (the question posits "integers", but it's easy to see that n must be positive and m might as well be assumed to be positive). Forgive my change of variable names, it's a bit more common this way. Let's make a few quick observations: First of all, the left hand side is always odd, therefore the right hand side must also be odd, which means that m must be odd. Remember that. We will need it, down the line. Another thing we should do when looking at such equations is just try out some small numbers. We immediately find two solutions: 3^1 = 1^2+2 3^3 = 5^2+2 . Further attempts don't seem to yield anything, so we are led to hypothesize that these are the only solutions. This turns out to be the case, but we have some work to do in order to prove it. Theorem: If m,n are positive integers and 3^n=m^2+2 then either (m,n)=(1,1) or (m,n)=(5,3) . Note : if you're familiar with basic notions of algebraic number theory, the first half of the proof is quite short and straightforward. The long tale below is not meant to be a compact proof, but rather a motivated investigation into this equation and the way algebraic number theory is naturally born as a result of such investigations. Step 1: Factoring the Right Hand Side Consider the equation again: 3^n = m^2+2 . On the left we have a product (of 3's), and on the right we have a sum. It's hard to compare products and sums, so our first goal is to turn the expression on the right into a product as well. Trouble is, we don't know how to factor m^2+2 . In school you've learned that m^2-1 = (m-1)(m+1) , for instance, but you may have been told that m^2+2 is "irreducible". Well, it is — over the rational numbers. But if we introduce the complex number \sqrt{-2} , then m^2+2 factors right away: \displaystyle m^2+2 = (m+\sqrt{-2})(m-\sqrt{-2}) . We are therefore led to switch the domain of discourse from mere integers into the realm of numbers of the form a+b\sqrt{-2} where a,b are integers. Why a+b\sqrt{-2} and not some other expression? And why do we insist that a,b should be integers? Well, we need \sqrt{-2} to factor our right hand side, and we want to do arithmetic — we're going to need to add, subtract and multiply. So our best bet is to start with the integers we know and love, throw in \sqrt{-2} , and then keep adding and subtracting and multiplying things until we stop finding any new numbers. The result is the set of numbers a+b\sqrt{-2} where a,b are arbitrary integers. You can easily verify that adding, subtracting and multiplying two numbers of this form yields another number of the same form. For example, \displaystyle (2+3\sqrt{-2})(4+5\sqrt{-2}) = 8+10\sqrt{-2}+12\sqrt{-2}+15\cdot (-2) = = -22+22\sqrt{-2} . Like the integers, these numbers cannot always be divided by each other. For example, we just saw that -22+22\sqrt{-2} is divisible by 4+5\sqrt{-2} , and the quotient is 2+3\sqrt{-2} . But you can see that -21+22\sqrt{-2} is not divisible by 4+5\sqrt{-2} , because there will be a remainder of 1 left over. To be sure, try solving (a+b\sqrt{-2})(4+5\sqrt{-2})=-21+22\sqrt{-2} and observe that no integers a,b make this true. If we allow a,b to be arbitrary real or complex numbers, we can no longer do arithmetic. Everything can be divided by everything else and we have too much freedom. Our goal is to prove that a certain equation has no solutions in integers other than the ones we know. We should stay as close to integers as we can. The set of numbers of the form a+b\sqrt{-2} is an example of a "commutative ring" , which is a collection of things that can be added, subtracted and multiplied with the usual rules of arithmetic still applying (for instance x(y+z)=xy+xz .) This particular ring is named the ring of integers of \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-2}) , or \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-2}] , but we will simply call it R . As soon as you come across a ring like R you should immediately investigate its number theoretic properties: its primes, its units (things that can be multiplied by something to yield 1), whether it has unique factorization, etc. We will investigate these properties as we need them here, because one of the things I hope to do is reveal why number theorists care about these things. Step 2: Oh look, the Left Hand Side got Factored as well Let's go back to our equation. It now looks like this: \displaystyle 3^n = (m+\sqrt{-2})(m-\sqrt{-2}) . This looks very promising. Why? Well, imagine we were working with the ordinary integers, and we were looking at the equation 3^n = ab . We can immediately conclude from this that a,b must both be powers of 3. Right? Neither of them can have any other prime factor; if a were divisible by 17, then the product ab would also be divisible by 17, but 3^n is not divisible by 17, obviously. So we can conclude that a,b are both powers of 3. Can we do the same here? Hopefully not! We are looking at 3^n = (m+\sqrt{-2})(m-\sqrt{-2}) and neither of the things on the right looks anything like a power of 3. That would have been ok if we thought our equation has no solutions at all, but it does! So how come, for example, that 3^1=1^2+2 works? Does it not contradict our factorization? Let's see what happens when n=m=1 : \displaystyle 3^1 = (1+\sqrt{-2})(1-\sqrt{-2}) . Oh. Bummer. Over the ordinary integers, 3^n=ab implies that a,b must be powers of 3, but in our ring R this obviously is no longer the case. You see, when we elevated the discussion from integers into R , we managed to factor not only our right-hand side, but inadvertently our left-hand side as well... Indeed, \displaystyle 3 = (1+\sqrt{-2})(1-\sqrt{-2}) so \displaystyle 3^n = (1+\sqrt{-2})^n(1-\sqrt{-2})^n . Ok. So really, our equation in R is (1+\sqrt{-2})^n(1-\sqrt{-2})^n = (m+\sqrt{-2})(m-\sqrt{-2}) . This is still very promising. On the left we have a product (of n th powers), and on the right we have a product. It looks like this: A^n B^n = XY . It would be really nice if we could argue that X must be A^n and Y must be B^n (or vice versa). If that were so, we would know that (1+\sqrt{-2})^n = m+\sqrt{-2} , and we could investigate the powers of 1+\sqrt{-2} to see that they are very rarely of this form. This will indeed be our final step, but first we have to ensure that we can actually draw that conclusion. Discussion: When One Product Equals Another If you have one product that equals another product, can you conclude that the factors are the same? Well, it's not that simple. Suppose I tell you that AB=XY . Can you infer that X=A and Y=B (or the other way around)? There are several ways this can fail; some pretty obvious, some more subtle. One obvious way is this: consider 3 \times 4 = 2 \times 6 . Two different pairs of numbers have the same product. How does this happen? Well, the number 12 can be broken down into prime factors as 12=2 \times 2 \times 3 , and we can group these factors in different ways to get (2 \times 2) \times 3 or 2 \times (2 \times 3) . So, if you just know that AB = XY , you should be worried if A,B,X,Y can further be broken down into products of smaller things. What if the numbers involved cannot be broken down into products? There's another problem: every number can be written as a product in silly ways. For example, if I told you that 2 \times 3 = XY , despite the fact that 2 and 3 are prime, you still couldn't infer that X,Y=2,3 . Maybe X,Y=1,6 ? Or X,Y=-1, -6 ? We have to ensure that our numbers can't be units , which are things like 1 or -1 that can be multiplied together to make 1's. We can always plug 1's and -1's into products. Ok, but there's another, even most subtle difficulty. suppose I tell you that AB=XY , and I promise you that none of these numbers is a unit, and that all of these numbers are irreducible, meaning they cannot further be split into products. Now we should be able to conclude that A,B and X,Y are the same numbers, right? Right? Well, yes... provided unique factorization holds true. This is a very familiar property of ordinary integers: When you write down a number, such as 92, as a product of primes, as in 92 = 2 \times 2 \times 23 , you know that there's one and only one way to do that. You can't find some other way of writing 92 as a product of primes, as in " 92 = 7 \times 13 ". This last equality is false, thankfully. But how do we know this can't happen? Incredibly, when we venture out beyond the integers, it can happen. For example if we work with the numbers a+b\sqrt{-5} where a,b are integers, then 2 \times 3 = (1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5}) , and all of the numbers here are irreducible: they cannot be broken down into products any further. In the ring \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}] , unique factorization doesn't hold. (In 1847, a guy called Gabriel Lamé announced a proof of Fermat's Last Theorem. It was wrong, and the reason it was wrong was that he implicitly assumed unique factorization holds in rings where it does not). Incidentally, when unique factorization fails, we have to make a careful distinction between "irreducible numbers" which can't be written as products and "prime numbers" which divide a product only when they divide one of the factors. Luckily, in our ring R , this will not be a concern. Step 4: Analyzing the Product in Our Ring Let's go back to our equation. (1+\sqrt{-2})^n(1-\sqrt{-2})^n = (m+\sqrt{-2})(m-\sqrt{-2}) . We want to infer that (1+\sqrt{-2})^n = m \pm \sqrt{-2} , one of the factors on the right. As we shall see, this is a very powerful conclusion. So we are faced with the following challenges: 1. Show that 1+\sqrt{-2} and 1-\sqrt{-2} are irreducible (or "primes", which in our ring is the same thing). This means they cannot be broken further, so the right hand side must be a certain grouping of n copies of each. 2. Show that m+\sqrt{-2} and m-\sqrt{-2} are relatively prime, meaning they have no common factors, and that they are not units. If we show this, then each of them must be the product of n copies of one of the irreducible elements on the left. 3. Finally, we must show that the numbers in R have unique factorization into primes. To do all these things, there's a very useful trick called the norm . If you're familiar with complex numbers, you know that each complex number z has a size or absolute value |z| , and one nice thing about it is that the size of a product is the product of the sizes . This is helpful because it lets us show that certain products can't work because the sizes don't work. This is often easier. Even if you're not familiar with complex numbers, you can directly show that defining the norm N(a+b\sqrt{-2}) = (a+b\sqrt{-2})(a-b\sqrt{-2}) = a^2+2b^2 achieves the following things: - For any number x in R , the norm N(x) is an ordinary non-negative integer. - For any two numbers x,y in R , the norm satisfies N(xy)=N(x)N(y) . The norm of a product is the product of the norms. - Therefore, if x divides y then N(x) divides N(y) . - Contrariwise, if N(x) doesn't divide N(y) then x does not divide y . Armed with this device, we can quickly dispose of our challenges. For starters, what are the units in R ? Luckily, the only ones are the good old 1 and -1. Why? Well, if xy=1 then N(x)N(y)=1 . But the norm is a non-negative integer, which means that N(x)=N(y)=1 . When does a^2+2b^2=1 ? Obviously, b=0 and a = \pm 1 are the only solutions. (This is really fortunate. In other rings, there are many non-obvious units, like for example (17+12\sqrt{2})(17-12\sqrt{2})=1 . This is one of the main reasons why imaginary quadratic number fields are so much easier than real quadratic number fields. Units are a major nuisance). Now, what about primes? Determining the primes completely takes some work, but there's a simple condition that helps: if a number has a prime norm, it must be irreducible. For if it were reducible, its norm would be the product of the norms of its factors. Since N(1+\sqrt{-2})=3 and N(1-\sqrt{-2})=3 , both of these numbers are irreducible. This is great: the left hand side of our equation is a genuine prime decomposition. There are no further hidden factors. Next: why are m+\sqrt{-2} and m-\sqrt{-2} relatively prime? Imagine that some prime number p in R divided both of them. Then it would also divide their difference, which is 2\sqrt{-2} = (\sqrt{-2})^3 . The only prime which divides (\sqrt{-2})^3 is \sqrt{-2} , a number of norm 2 . But the norm of m+\sqrt{-2} is m^2+2 , and if you scroll up to the distant beginning of this answer you'll remember that m is odd, so m^2+2 is odd, so it cannot be divisible by 2 . Success! The prime \sqrt{-2} cannot divide m+\sqrt{-2} , and it is the only candidate for dividing both it and m-\sqrt{-2} . So, the factors on the right hand side of our equation are relatively prime, and none of them is a unit (look at their norms), so we can finally conclude that one of them must be none other than (1+\sqrt{-2})^n itself. But wait — we still haven't proved that R has unique factorization into primes. If it doesn't, nothing we said makes sense. I'll need to leave this part out for now since this answer is horribly long as it is; suffice to say that this follows quickly from the fact that we have in R an analog of the idea of "division with remainder", and the norm of the remainder is always smaller than the norm of the divisor. From this property we can infer that it has unique factorization much like we do this for ordinary integers. Step 5: Powers of 1+\sqrt{-2} We've made an important discovery: One of m+\sqrt{-2} or m-\sqrt{-2} must be (1+\sqrt{-2})^n . How does this help? Instead of our original equation, which was 3^n=m^2+2 , we now have \displaystyle \left(1+\sqrt{-2}\right)^n = m \pm \sqrt{-2} . Why is that progress? Here's the thing: first of all, on the right we no longer have m^2 , just m . That's a much easier thing to work with; we don't need to worry about it being a square or not. Secondly, we can start looking at powers of 1+\sqrt{-2} , and see whether they do or don't look like something plus or minus \sqrt{-2} . When they don't, the equation has no solution. Those powers are very concrete numbers. We can calculate them successively quite simply, by multiplying each one by 1+\sqrt{-2} to get the next one: (1+\sqrt{-2})^1 = 1+\sqrt{-2} (1+\sqrt{-2})^2 = -1+2 \sqrt{-2} (1+\sqrt{-2})^3= -5+\sqrt{-2} (1+\sqrt{-2})^4 = -7 -4 \sqrt{-2} (1+\sqrt{-2})^5 = 1 - 11 \sqrt{-2} (1+\sqrt{-2})^6 = 23 - 10 \sqrt{-2} We observe two powers here which indeed have a mere \sqrt{-2} as the b part: n=1 and n=3 . This is excellent news - those are exactly the powers that yield solutions to our original equation. The other powers all have much larger coefficients in front of the \sqrt{-2} . Therefore, our goal is now to prove than when n>3 , the number \displaystyle \left(1+\sqrt{-2}\right)^n = a_n + b_n \sqrt{-2} has b_n \neq \pm 1 . For example, b_4 = -4 , b_5 = -11 , and so on; all of these numbers, we must show, are never 1 or -1 (except for b_1 and b_3 ). Showing that b_n can't be -1 is relatively easy. If you write down the sequence b_n and consider the residues modulo 11, you get 0, 1, 2, 1, 7, 0, 1, 2, 1, 7, \ldots . It's not hard to show using induction that this is periodic behavior continues forever. Since the residue -1 (or 10) modulo 11 never shows up, b_n can never be -1. From here on we will focus on showing that b_n can't be 1 as soon as n > 3 . Since reduction mod 11 was so useful, we may wonder about reducing the sequence modulo other things. Playing around with various options you may find that the reductions modulo 2, 4, 8, 16 etc. seem promising: the sequence b_n modulo 2^r seems to always be periodic with period 2^r , and the residue 1 only shows up in positions 1 and 3 in the period. As you increase r , the positions of the 1's move farther and farther out, and if we can prove that this is the case, we're done. (Note: I am indebted to math.stackexchange user Achille Hui for helping me complete this part of the solution). Let's apply the binomial theorem to the expression (1+\sqrt{-2})^n . We get \displaystyle \left(1+\sqrt{-2}\right)^n = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}\sqrt{-2}^k . In this sum, when k is even we get an ordinary integer, and when k is odd we get an integer times \sqrt{-2} . We only care about those, because we only care about the b_n s. So we can write k=2t+1 and obtain the following formula for our b_n s: \displaystyle b_n = \sum_{t=0}^{\lfloor \frac{n-1}{2} \rfloor} \binom{n}{2t+1}(-1)^t2^t . The strange upper bound of this sum is simply meant to ensure that 2t+1 doesn't exceed n . Don't worry too much about it. We can write this in a more friendly way like this: b_n = \binom{n}{1} - 2\binom{n}{3} + 4\binom{n}{5} - 8\binom{n}{7} - \ldots . This is just an alternating sum of binomial coefficients multiplied by some powers of 2. The scary part about this formula is that it gets longer and longer as n grows. But there's hope: remember we thought it would be useful to consider the residues of b_n mod powers of 2. If we're looking at things mod 32, everything in this formula except the first five elements vanishes. In fact, if we're lucky and the binomial coefficients contribute more powers of 2, then even more elements disappear. This will be our proof strategy. First of all, if n is even, everything on the right is even, so b_n is even and cannot be equal to 1 . So we may assume that n is odd. Since n is odd, it is something even plus 1. The "something even" is divisible by 2 a certain number of times, and since powers of 2 are important here we need to know exactly how many times. So we write n=2^r u+1 with u odd. Now, when t>0 , \binom{n}{2t+1} = \frac{n(n-1)}{2t(2t+1)}\binom{n-2}{2t-1} . In the numerator we have an odd number n and then an even number n-1 which is divisible by 2 r times. In the denominator we have 2t+1 , which is odd, and 2t which is even and we have no idea just how even, meaning how many powers of 2 it contains. But remember that in the formula for b_n there's another ingredient, those powers of 2 which are represented by 2^t . As soon as t is more than 2, 2^t has more 2's than 2t . In other words, the expression 2^t\binom{n}{2t+1} is divisible by 2 at least r+1 times: r times come from n-1 and at least one more from \frac{2^t}{2t} . So, if we work modulo 2^{r+1} , we can ignore everything with t>2 , that is everything except the very first few terms: b_n \equiv \binom{n}{1}-2\binom{n}{3}+4\binom{n}{5} \pmod{2^{r+1}} . The good news here are that our long formula has been reduced to just three terms. Three terms we can handle! In fact at this point, a routine check shows that if r>1 , that is if n-1 is divisible by at least 4, then b_n cannot equal 1 modulo 2^{r+1} , which means that it cannot be equal to 1, period. If however r=1 , this argument isn't enough. But if n-1 isn't divisible by 4, then n-3 is, so we write n=2^r u+3 (those are now different u and r ) and we repeat the argument. I'll leave the details to you, gentle reader who made it all the way down here. Putting all these pieces together, we've shown that the sequence b_n never returns to 1 (or -1) once n > 3 . This means that (1+\sqrt{-2})^n is never of the form m \pm \sqrt{-2} for n>3 , which using the discoveries we made in the ring R means that 3^n cannot equal m^2+2 once n>3 . And this, finally, proves the theorem. QED
how-do-i-solve-this-int-0-1-sqrt-x-sqrt-: How do I solve this  \int_{0}^{1} \sqrt{x+\sqrt{x+\sqrt{x+....}}} dx ?  — Whatever function f(x) is represented by the infinite nested radical \displaystyle f(x)=\sqrt{x+\sqrt{x+\sqrt{x+\cdots}}} we can reasonably expect it to satisfy \displaystyle \sqrt{x+f(x)}=f(x) This is because what follows the first “ x+ ” in the nested radical is precisely the same nested radical. The functional equation can be squared to yield x+f(x)=f(x)^2 which is a quadratic equation in the unknown function f , and can be solved just like any quadratic equation. We find: \displaystyle f(x)=\frac{1}{2}\left(1\pm\sqrt{1+4x}\right) At this point we may be unsure about the correct sign to pick for that \pm thingie. It may even be a different choice for different values of x . Notice, however, that for any 0<x\le 1 , the sequence \displaystyle \sqrt{x},\sqrt{x+\sqrt{x}},\sqrt{x+\sqrt{x+\sqrt{x}}},\ldots is monotonically increasing and bounded (by, say, 2 ), so it converges, and its limit is positive. Therefore we conclude that \displaystyle f(x)=\frac{1}{2}\left(1+\sqrt{1+4x}\right) (This doesn’t work at x=0 , since then the sequence is not monotonically increasing and simply stays put. But the value at a single point doesn’t affect the integral.) Finally, the integral is elementary: \displaystyle \int_0^1 f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{5}{12}\left(1+\sqrt{5}\right)
what-is-an-example-of-a-conjecture-that-: What is an example of a conjecture that was proven wrong for "very large" numbers? — 12 isn't prime: it's composite. So is 121. So is 1211. So is 12111. So is 121111. So is 1211111. So is 12111111. This seems to be a persistent pattern. Let's keep going. Seven 1’s, composite. Eight, still composite. Nine. Ten, eleven and twelve. We keep going. Everything up to twenty 1’s is composite. Up to thirty, still everything is composite. Forty. Fifty. Keep going. One hundred . They are all composite. At this point it may seem reasonable to conjecture that these numbers are never prime. But this isn't true. The number with 138 digits, all 1’s except for the second digit which is 2, is prime. To be clear, this isn't a particularly shocking example. It's not really that surprising. But it underscores the fact that some very simple patterns in numbers persist into pretty big territory, and then suddenly break down. There appear to be two slightly different questions here. One is about statements which appear to be true, and are verifiably true for small numbers, but turn out to be false where the first counterexamples are massive. The other question is about such situations which have furthermore become actual conjectures, put forth and studied and perhaps widely believed in, until they were refuted. In response to such questions, I used to cite a couple of nice examples given by Stark in his number theory textbook, by way of motivating his readers to see the need for proofs. One example is Pólya’s conjecture , which is a famous instance of this phenomenon: it was a real conjecture suggested by a very prominent mathematician, supported by both numerical evidence and heuristic reasoning, which turned out to be false. Another example given by Stark is a nice, smallish Diophantine equation which has a very large smallest solution. This isn't a case of a genuine conjecture, but it nicely demonstrates the necessity for proofs. In that spirit, my new go-to example is definitely this gem . If you check numerically, you will quickly convince yourself that there aren't any natural numbers which satisfy \displaystyle \frac{a}{b+c}+\frac{b}{a+c}+\frac{c}{a+b}=4 . You can search through millions, billions, trillions or quadrillions if you have the resources, and nothing works. It would seem very reasonable to expect that there aren't any solutions to this simple equation in natural numbers, just like many other similar equations. But that's false. There are infinitely many solutions, and the smallest one is ginormous . This, to be clear, is not an instance of a “genuine conjecture”. I don't believe anyone actually suggested that this equation has no solutions: by the time it was stumbled upon, there was already enough theory to solve it. But it is a fantastic example of an equation which seems unsolvable unless you look very, very far. I don't know if it was ever formally suggested that \text{Li}(x) , the logarithmic integral, is always greater than \pi(x) , the number of primes less than x . The Prime Number Theorem says that the ratio between these two functions approaches 1 , but numerical evidence seems to strongly suggest that while this is of course true, it is consistently the logarithmic integral which has the upper hand. This is indeed true for values of x up to billions, and likely much further. But Littlewood proved that these two functions switch sides infinitely often. It's just that the first reversal occurs very, very far out. Littlewood’s student Skewes showed that it happens earlier than e^{e^{e^{79}}} , a number now known as Skewes’ number. Today it is known that it happens earlier, but still the first occurrence is gigantic. Once again, I'm not sure if this was ever an “official” conjecture which got refuted, but it would have been a very reasonable conjecture to make even if it weren't. A better example perhaps is Mertens’ conjecture from 1885, refuted exactly one hundred years later. The Möbius function is an important function in number theory and combinatorics. It is defined as \mu(n)=(-1)^k if n has k distinct prime factors, and 0 otherwise (when n has a repeated factor). The Mertens function is then M(n)=\sum_{k=1}^n \mu(k) . As early as 1885, Stieltjes conjectured that |M(n)|<\sqrt{n} for all n , and this is supported by overwhelming numerical evidence. Moreover, it implies the Riemann Hypothesis – so it was definitely an interesting conjecture. In 1897, Mertens independently conjectured it again. However, it's false. Odlyzko and te Riele proved in 1985 that M(n) exceeds \sqrt{n} by at least 6% infinitely many times. The first counterexample is probably around 10^{40} or so. Finally, I'll mention a less elementary example, but one which (to me) was quite a shocker. For any finite group G we can form the group algebra \mathbb{Z}G , which is just the free abelian group generated by the elements of G , with multiplication of basis elements defined as in G and then extended linearly. If you don't know what any of that means, you'll need to take my word for it: finite groups are among the most fundamental building blocks of math, and group algebras are a very natural, and extremely useful, construction involving them. We may then wonder: the group determines its group algebra – is the opposite also true? Can you recover the group from the group algebra? In other words, if \mathbb{Z}G \cong \mathbb{Z}H , does it follow that G \cong H ? This was not a named conjecture, but it was definitely a conjecture. It is mentioned, for example, in Isaacs’ “Character Theory of Finite Groups” from 1976 (p. 41 in my edition). It turns out to be false, as Martin Hertweck showed in a 2001 paper [1] titled “A Counterexample to the Isomorphism Problem for Integral Group Rings”. His counterexample is a group of size 2^{21}97^{28} , and people can be forgiven for taking long to find it. Footnotes [1] A Counterexample to the Isomorphism Problem for Integral Group Rings
is-it-difficult-to-prove-fermat-s-last-t:
Is it difficult to prove Fermat's Last Theorem for case n=3? — “Difficult” is in the eye of the besolver. “Fermat’s Last Theorem” (FLT) for exponent 3 is the statement that a^3+b^3=c^3 has no solutions in nonzero integers. It would make a very difficult puzzle for the vast majority of high-schoolers, even those who excel at math olympiads such as the IMO. It’s not an easy problem to solve from first principles, as you can plainly see by the unreasonable length of this very Quora answer. However, proofs of this theorem have been around for over 200 years now, and they are very well understood and not hard to follow if you have the necessary background. They are considered quite elementary, as mathematical proofs go, and every serious student of number theory is expected to understand them well, and even be able to produce them from scratch if necessary. I wouldn’t call this an “easy” theorem: Even with the full machinery of algebraic number theory, it is still a little intricate. But I also wouldn’t call something “difficult” if it is done in a few pages in almost every textbook on the subject (Wiles’ proof of the Taniyama-Shimura-Weil conjecture, now that’s difficult.) It'll be good for the proof to be on Quora, so let’s do it. But first, a bit of history. Contrary to massively prevailing popular belief, Fermat never stated his “last theorem” that a^n+b^n=c^n has no nonzero integer solutions when n>2 . In none of his many writings and letters did he ever claim to know how to prove it. The famous marginal note (“which the margin is too narrow to hold”) was published by his son after his death, and if indeed Fermat did write it, he never once repeated that claim in public or in correspondence. He did state the cases of exponent 3 and 4 quite often, and put them forth as a challenge to his contemporaries, starting around 1636. We don’t know if he actually knew how to prove the case n=3 . He published a proof for n=4 , which is much easier. The fascinating history of the misunderstanding of the circumstances of the birth of FLT is probably out of scope for this question, but you can see some of the highlights here . At any rate, Fermat wasn’t the first person (loc. cit.) to consider the equation a^3+b^3=c^3 , but he certainly made it famous. The first serious claim for a proof was put forward by Euler. As early as 1753 he claimed to have one (in a letter to Goldbach [1] , dated August 4), but the first known written account of it is in his “Vollständige Anleitung zur Algebra ” from 1770, and it is incomplete. Most experts believe he did have a complete proof (the gap can be filled with results from a 1760 paper of his), or at least he would have been able to produce one had the gap been pointed out to him. See Bergmann [2] and Mačys [3] . As of this writing, the Wikipedia article which discusses proofs of FLT for small exponents covers the case n=3 with reference to “A crucial lemma” that is nowhere proven, and this is indeed the same gap present in Euler’s 1770 proof. It is possible to close this gap with a careful analysis of the quadratic form X^2+3Y^2 , but in the proof I reproduce below I will take a more modern approach, closer to Gauss’ proof. Gauss, it should be noted, was not a huge fan of FLT. In an 1816 letter to Olbers he wrote (see Ribenboim [4] ): I confess that Fermat's theorem as an isolated proposition has very little interest for me, because I could easily lay down a multitude of such propositions, which one could neither prove nor dispose of. I think it is useful for modern students to understand this. FLT in and of itself (“as an isolated proposition”) is indeed quite devoid of interest. Of course, its legendary status motivated many prominent mathematicians to attack it, thereby developing magnificent theories that would apply to countless other problems and create the whole field of modern number theory. Alright, enough history. Let’s get started. Outline The plan of attack is a very common one in number theory. We have an equation that looks like some high power which is equal to the sum of various things: X^n = A+B+C+\ldots We attempt to factor the right hand side so that it becomes a product, rather than a sum. X^n = F\cdot G\cdot H \cdots Then, we try to show that F, G, H and so on are relatively prime, which would force each of them to itself be an n^	ext{th} power. This usually turns out to be a very strong requirement which is either outright impossible, or it can be used to yield a smaller solution of the original equation. Indeed, since we managed to show that F itself is some x^n , we may be able to manipulate things to have x^n=a+b+c+\ldots which is an equation that looks very much like the one we’ve started with, but clearly, with a smaller x than X had been. By “infinite descent”, we reach a contradiction: if any solution existed, there would be one with minimal X , contradicting the descent step. In order to carry out the first step, factoring the right-hand side, we typically need to move up from plain old integers into some number ring , which is a set of complex numbers that includes the usual integers but with a whole lot of new and exciting ones, and where many (though not all) of the rules of arithmetic still apply. In our case, the equation is X^3=Y^3+Z^3 Of course, we can also write it as Z^3=X^3-Y^3 = (X-Y)(X^2+XY+Y^2) which partially factors the right-hand side. A slightly different factorization was used by Euler, but this still left him with the gap of having to analyze the quadratic forms that emerge. Here, we prefer to factor the thing completely , by introducing a cube root of unity. The Eisenstein Integers The complex numbers are usually defined as the set of expressions a+bi where a,b are real numbers and i is a new entity satisfying i^2=-1 . We will now do something very similar by introducing an entity \omega and looking at the expressions a+b\omega where a,b are integers while \omega satisfies \omega^3=1 but \omega 
eq 1 . Note well: a,b are integers now, not arbitrary real numbers. The set of all such expressions makes up a ring we will call R . It is a “ring” because you can add, subtract and multiply those numbers, but not necessarily divide them, much like the integers \mathbb{Z} themselves. The elements of R are sometimes called Eisenstein Integers in honor of Gotthold Eisenstein , one of the 19th century’s mathematical superstars who didn’t live to be 30 years old. If you’re comfortable with complex numbers, you can simply take \omega to be \displaystyle \omega = e^{2 \pi i /3} =  rac{-1+i\sqrt{3}}{2} The numbers a+b\omega then look like this , in the complex plane: The Eisenstein integers are the red/green dots (the red ones are the “units”, as we will shortly explain). Pay special attention to that green 1-\omega sitting there at the lower right; we will be using it a lot. To get comfortable working with Eisenstein integers you must first notice a very important property of the number \omega : \omega^2+\omega+1=0 . This follows immediately from the fact that \omega^3-1=0 , which is the same as (\omega-1)(\omega^2+\omega+1)=0 . Since we decreed that \omega 
eq 1 , it must make the other factor vanish. Of course, if you consider \omega to be the complex number e^{2 \pi i /3} , you can also just prove this directly. This property of \omega is the reason we can settle for a+b\omega , and we don’t need to look at things like a+b\omega+c\omega^2 . Indeed, whenever an \omega^2 emerges, you can just replace it with -\omega-1 . With that, you can start playing around with Eisenstein integers. (2+\omega)+(3-4\omega) = 5-3\omega (5+\omega)(2-3\omega)=10+2\omega-15\omega-3\omega^2=10-13\omega+3(\omega+1)=13-10\omega Once you get used to them, Eisenstein integers are no more mysterious than ordinary integers, but they are much more good-looking. The integers are just boring, equally-spaced dots on the number line, but the Eisensteins are such a pretty lattice, aren’t they? Here, for example, are the Eisenstein primes, to be defined shortly: Arithmetic in R From now on, when we say “number”, we mean an Eisenstein integer, meaning an element of R . Since those numbers can be added, subtracted and multiplied, we can migrate all the standard definitions of arithmetic and try to understand what becomes of them. Here are all of the things we will need. Some of these may look familiar, some probably not. If x,y are numbers, we will say that x divides y if there is some number m such that mx=y . This is the exact same definition you’re used to for the ordinary integers. We will write x\mid y when x divides y . For example, earlier we’ve noticed that (5+\omega)\mid (13-10\omega) , and also (2-3\omega)\mid (13-10\omega) . We say that x and y are congruent modulo m , written x\equiv y \pmod{m} , if m divides the difference x-y . This is, again, the exact same definition as the one for ordinary integers, but now all three participants ( x,y and m ) are allowed to be “new” numbers: elements of R . If x\mid 1 we say that x is a unit . We don’t usually talk about “units” in school arithmetic, because we usually do school arithmetic with positive integers only, and then the only unit is 1 itself. But among the integers we already have two units: 1 and -1 , and it’s useful to call them out. In our new number system we actually have six of them, so they certainly deserve a name. The units can also be thought of as the invertible elements of R : they are the only numbers who have a multiplicative inverse. You should go ahead and prove that 1,-1,\omega,-\omega,1+\omega and -1-\omega are all units. They are, in fact, the only ones. If x\mid y and y\mid x we will say that x and y are associates , and write x \sim y . This is also not usually explained in school arithmetic, because among positive integers two numbers are associates only if they are the same, and it seems silly to define something that’s just another way of saying “equal”. However, if you think about arithmetic among the integers, you’ll notice that 7|(-7) and (-7)|7 , so 7 and -7 are associates. In fact, you should prove that the associates of x are simply the products xu of x by some unit u , just like the associates of 7 are the products of 7 by \pm 1 in the ordinary integers. We say that x is irreducible if it is not a unit, but the only things dividing it are units and its associates. In other words, a non-unit x is irreducible if x=yz implies that either y or z are units, so the “factorization” is as useless as writing 17=(-1)(-17) . This should sound familiar: it is the usual definition of “prime” for ordinary integers. In ring theory, the correct term is irreducible, because “prime” is defined in a slightly different way. In our ring, the two terms mean the same thing, so we will simply call the irreducible elements primes . For every prime p and every number x , we can consider the highest power of p which divides x , or “the number of times” p divides x . This is called the p - valuation of x , denoted 	ext{val}_p(x) . It is a very simple notion but usually also excluded from school arithmetic, where we would have found that the 2 -valuation of 40 is 3 since 2^3 divides 40 but 2^4 does not. When k=	ext{val}_p(x) we write p^k\mid \mid x to denote that p^k\mid x but no higher power of p manages to divide x . So 2^3\mid \mid 40 , for example. Two numbers are called relatively prime if only units divide both of them. Again, this is exactly the same definition you’re used to from school arithmetic. If x=a+b\omega , we call  ar{x}=a+b\omega^2=(a-b)-b\omega the conjugate of x . The reason is that this is just the ordinary complex conjugate of x , and therefore the product N(x)=x ar{x} is always a positive integer, called the norm of x . You should work this out: show that N(a+b\omega)=a^2-ab+b^2 . Show that N(xy)=N(x)N(y) , and conclude that the units are precisely the numbers of norm 1 , and that numbers with a prime norm must be prime (warning: the converse isn’t true. The norm of 2 is 4 , but 2 is still prime among the Eisenstein integers). For any two numbers x,y a greatest common divisor (gcd) is a number d which divides both of them, and is divisible by any other number with that property. So d\mid x , d\mid y and if e\mid x and e\mid y then e\mid d . Notice how “greatest” shifted meaning from “largest” to “being divisible by all other contenders”. The size properties of the ordinary integers can also be migrated to the Eisenstein integers, using the norm (this is what “Euclidean domain” means), but greatest common divisors can be defined without reference to size, and that’s a useful observation. Notice that I wrote “a gcd” rather than “the gcd”: in the presence of units and associates, we shouldn’t expect the gcd to be unique. Every number can be written as a product of primes , and be so written in essentially just one way . This is the analogue of “unique factorization” of ordinary integers. The “essentially” means that you can (of course) introduce units into the factorization if you wish, and you can also rearrange the order of the primes, but that’s it. If the same number x is written in two ways as a product of units and primes, there will be the same primes showing up in both ways, and each will show up the same number of times. Proving the existence and uniqueness of factorization into primes isn’t hard using the norm we just defined. If you know some ring theory, you will recognize that R is a Euclidean domain , and hence a principal ideal domain , and hence a unique factorization domain . Finally, as promised, we are going to give 1-\omega a name: we’ll call it \lambda = 1-\omega . Now, try to work out the following (relatively easy) exercises: N(\lambda)=3 \lambda^2 \sim 3 \lambda is prime Every number x is congruent to -1,0 or 1 modulo \lambda . Hint: Take any number x=a+b\omega , divide it by \lambda , and then simplify the fraction by multiplying numerator and denominator by  ar{\lambda} . If the result is in R , the number x is divisible by \lambda to begin with. If it’s not, what happens if you add or subtract 1 from x ? This result should be seen as an analogue of the fact that among ordinary integers, every number is congruent to -1,0 or 1 modulo 3 . In our new numbers, \lambda plays a very similar role to 3 . Among ordinary integers, every cube x^3 is congruent to -1, 0 or 1 modulo 9 . This is a very useful fact in understanding cubes and their sums. Show the analogous result for Eisenstein integers: if \lambda 
mid x then the cube x^3 is congruent to -1 or 1 modulo \lambda^4 . As an illuminating aside, show that among ordinary integers, a^3+b^3=c^3 is impossible if none of a,b,c is divisible by 3 . Use the fact we just mentioned about cubes modulo 9 . This means that the so-called “First Case” of FLT is trivial for n=3 . The reason we are obsessed with \lambda is that we’re going to factor x^3+y^3 into (x+y)(x+\omega y)(x+\omega^2 y) . Assuming that x and y are themselves relatively prime, show that the only prime which could possibly divide both x+y and x+\omega y is \lambda . Remember, from the outline, that we are hoping to make the factors relatively prime, so we can conclude that each of them is a cube; this is a decisive step. The Proof If the world had been fair, having done all this great work to build the ring R and understand its arithmetic, the proof should now have been a walk in the park. But the world isn’t fair, highness, and the proof is still intricate. But it’s useful to realize that it is now, at the very least, not insanely creative or surprising: it follows the steps we outlined earlier fairly routinely. We will first make the problem a bit harder. Instead of showing that x^3+y^3=z^3 has no solution in R , we will show that for any unit u you care to pick, the equation x^3+y^3=uz^3 has no solution either. Why are we doing this? Well, when we “descend” from a potential solution to a smaller one, a unit may get introduced. Therefore the argument would break if we limited ourselves to the case u=1 , and it’s easier to allow ourselves that flexibility from the outset. Luckily, the enhanced equation is still unsolvable, making for a clean proof. So now, suppose that we have three numbers (meaning Eisenstein integers) x,y,z such that x^3+y^3=uz^3 . We may suppose that x,y and z are pairwise relatively prime: if some prime divides two of them, it must also divide the third, and we can eliminate it. If \lambda doesn’t divide any of x,y,z , we observe that it certainly doesn’t divide the unit u , so everything in this equation is \pm 1 modulo \lambda . But you can’t make \pm 1 \pm 1 = \pm 1 work, so that’s out of the question. \lambda must divide at least one of x,y or z , and in fact it’s exactly one of them since they’re pairwise relatively prime. We may assume that it is z that’s divisible by \lambda : if it’s x or y , the proof is quite the same. Looking at the equation modulo \lambda^4 , recall that you’ve shown that cubes that aren’t divisible by \lambda are actually \pm 1 modulo \lambda^4 . So now we have \pm 1 \pm 1 \equiv uz^3 \pmod{\lambda^4} Since \lambda doesn’t divide 2 , we must actually have 0 on the left here, and so \lambda divides z enough times to make z^3 divisible by \lambda^4 . This means that, in fact, \lambda^2\mid z . If \lambda\mid \mid z then z^3 would merely be divisible by \lambda^3 . Let’s summarize what we know. We have x^3+y^3=uz^3 and \lambda^2\mid z while \lambda 
mid xy . We now, at last, use the main feature of the Eisenstein ring to factor the left hand side: (x+y)(x+\omega y)(x+\omega^2 y) = uz^3 . You should check that this factorization works out by expanding it if you hadn’t seen it before. It’s really just the observation that 1+t^3=(1+t)(1+\omega t)(1+\omega^2 t) , applied to t=x/y . If a product of some things is a cube, and if the things are relatively prime, each of them must itself be a cube. As we’ve observed, the factors in our left-hand side may not be relatively prime, but the only possible prime that could divide a couple of them is \lambda . So the plan is to carefully count how many \lambda 's are everywhere, cancel them, and conclude that what’s left is all cubes. Since 	ext{val}_\lambda(z) \geq 2 , we must have 	ext{val}_\lambda(z^3) \geq 6 . This means that at least one of the three factors on the left must also be divisible by at least \lambda^2 , and we’re going to assume that it’s the x+y factor. Otherwise just replace y by \omega y or \omega^2 y . It’s very convenient that \omega is a unit. Now, x+\omega y = (x + y) - \lambda y . The first term, x+y , has \lambda -valuation at least 2 , but the second one, \lambda y , is only divisible by \lambda once. This means that the difference is also divisible by \lambda just once (this is the simple observation that a number divisible by 17^2 plus a number divisible by 17 but not 17^2 is only divisible by 17 . It’s the “ultrametric” property of valuations). The same is true for x+\omega^2 y , so each of these factors contributes just a single \lambda , and everything else must come from the x+y . In summary, 	ext{val}_\lambda(x+y) = 3 	ext{val}_\lambda(z) - 2 	ext{val}_\lambda(x+\omega y) = 1 	ext{val}_\lambda(x+\omega^2 y) = 1 Apart from those powers of \lambda , each of those factors must be a cube, and there may be whatever units everywhere. We call the first valuation, the big one, t , so we can write A=(x+y) = u_1 z_0^3 \lambda^t B=(x+\omega y) = u_2 x_1^3 \lambda C=(x+\omega^2 y) = u_3 y_1^3 \lambda The new numbers x_1,y_1,z_0 are pairwise relatively prime, and none of them is divisible by \lambda since we’ve separated out the precise amount of \lambda 's in each term. Now, behold: A+B\omega+C\omega^2 = 0 . This is simply because 1+\omega+\omega^2=0 . This now reads u_1 z_0^3 \lambda^t + \omega u_2 x_1^3 \lambda + \omega^2 u_3 y_1^3 \lambda=0 and we can, hooray, cancel out a \lambda : u_1 z_0^3 \lambda^{t-1} + \omega u_2 x_1^3 + \omega^2 u_3 y_1^3=0 Miraculously, t-1 = 3	ext{val}_\lambda(z)-3 is a multiple of 3 . Let’s call it t-1=3s . Let us call z_1=z_0 \lambda^s , and we have u_1 z_1^3 + u_2' x_1^3 + u_3' y_1^3 = 0 (We just gave \omega u_2 and \omega^2 u_3 new names; they are still units). Multiplying by the inverse of u_2' we can rearrange this into x_1^3+v y_1^3 = w z_1^3 where v and w are still units. This almost looks like our original equation; we just have an extra pesky unit in front of y_1^3 . Not to worry, reducing this equation modulo \lambda^2 yields \pm 1 \pm v \equiv 0 \pmod{\lambda^2} (Recall that z_1 is still divisible by \lambda ), which implies that v=\pm 1 (the other potential units don’t work out). Flip y_1 into -y_1 if needed and obtain x_1^3+y_1^3 = w z_1^3 which is exactly the equation we started with, but with a possibly different unit in front of the z_1^3 (this is why we insisted on proving the more general theorem), and with 	ext{val}_\lambda(z_1) strictly smaller than 	ext{val}_\lambda(z) . This is a contradiction, since the first thing we saw was that in any such equation we must have at least \lambda^2 dividing the third variable. This shows that the equation indeed has no solutions in Eisenstein integers, and so it certainly can’t have any plain old integer solutions, proving FLT for exponent 3 . QED!
