why-is-the-obvious-proof-of-the-four-col: Why is the obvious proof of the four colour map theorem, which says that any planar map can be coloured using only 4 colours, seemingly wrong? If 3 colours are all touching each other, then the 4th colour that touches all 3 must encircle one of them. — I'd like to offer a perspective that may help readers understand more clearly not only why this proof doesn't work, but what is it about this kind of approach that makes it unlikely to succeed. At a high level, the question proposes a local approach to a global question. We have a map with many bordering countries: there might by ten, fifty or two million of them. The four-color theorem claims that no matter how large or intricate the map is, four colors always suffice to paint the countries such that neighboring countries have different colors. Notice that this is a claim about the entire map, not about this or that region of it. The entire map can be colored using just four colors. The argument proposed in the question is a local one. It says "whenever three colors are all touching each other, then... <something good happens>". The problem with such arguments is that they are demonstrably too good to be true . A map (or more generally, a graph) can require very few colors locally while requiring many colors globally, because we can't piece together the easy workarounds suggested by the local methods. Here's an example. Consider the following map: It has nine "countries" arranged in a circle, each one bordering just two others. For our discussion we can assume that the inner circle (and the outer region around the countries) aren't countries at all, so we don't need to worry about coloring them. If this bothers you, feel free to add them both as countries; they will require one more color and the discussion doesn't change. How many colors are required locally ? Obviously, just two. If you focus your attention on any country and its neighbors, or even its neighbors' neighbors, and even if you look far and consider the neighbors of these neighbors' neighbors, you only need two colors. Just use an alternating pattern: two colors are enough here... and also here... ...and here, too. So two colors suffice locally, in the vicinity of any single country. And those local colorings seem to cover the entire map, so... surely the map requires just two colors? Of course the answer is No. Those local colorings disagree with each other, and the only way to color the entire map is to use a third color: The need for this extra color arises due to a global feature of the map. Locally we need just two colors, but globally we need three. If there had been 100 countries in this cycle, two colors would work great. But if there are 101, you need three colors. The deciding factor here is the parity of the number of countries, and the parity is a global attribute: you can't determine if the number of countries is even or odd by looking at a certain horizon around each country. You have to scan all of them . The four-color theorem asserts that for a planar map, those global mismatches can always be resolved using just four colors. This is very, very far from obvious. Perhaps you can prove that four colors suffice around this country, and four colors also suffice around that country, and also over there ... but can you piece together all those local colorings into one global coloring ? How do you prove that you can? In a way, the actual proof of the 4CT does investigate local structures, and it proves that they can be resolved coherently. But the approach is not only more subtle, it actually requires the analysis of thousands of local structures and resolution methods. This is why it is, notoriously, one of the few mathematical proofs that absolutely requires a computer in order to be surveyed and verified.
what-is-the-value-of-sum-n-0-infty-binom: What is the value of \sum_{n=0}^\infty \binom{34}{4n}? — Oh my, what a fun question! Seriously, I have a whole new math circle plan just as a result of solving this gem. Very nice. Despite appearances, this isn’t actually a rote calculation problem. It is designed to teach you something, if you’re attuned to its sinister machinations. Merely tackling this question may give you a glimpse of harmonic analysis, or Fourier analysis on Abelian groups, or group character theory, or DFT and digital signal processing. Here’s the thing. You may be familiar with other, simpler sums involving binomial coefficients. \displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}=2^n \tag 1 \displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}(-1)^k=0 \tag 2 (The second one requires n>0 ). Those are well-known, and have many proofs. The proof that interests us now is one you may have seen in school. It goes like this: \displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}X^k = (X+1)^n \tag 3 This is just a simple instance of the binomial theorem. Now, all you have to do is substitute X=1 to get (1), while X=-1 gives you (2), immediately. Easy. Evidently, the identity (3) is a lot more powerful than (1) and (2). It shows that we can calculate sums of binomial coefficients weighted by powers of any fixed number X (in other words, we understand a generating function, which is always a useful thing.) However, in and of itself this doesn’t seem to be helpful here. The weights we want are 1,0,0,0,1,0,0,0,1,0,0,0,\ldots since we wish to keep just the binomial coefficients \binom{n}{k} where k is divisible by 4 . And unfortunately, there’s no X whose powers look like that. What do we do? Fourier transform, that’s what we do. You see, the sequence 1,0,0,0,1,0,0,0,\ldots is not a sequence of powers of one number, yet it is periodic with a period of 4 (it’s an “impulse train” for signal processing people). If we find enough sequences of period 4 which are powers of a single number then, with luck, we may be able to combine them to yield the sequence we want. What sequences are available to us? We have the constant sequence (“powers of 1”, or the “DC offset” in engineering parlance, or the “trivial character”) 1,1,1,1,1,1,\ldots We have the powers of -1 1,-1,1,-1,1,-1\ldots and of course, the only two numbers whose powers are sequences of period 4 are the imaginary units i and -i , yielding the sequences 1,i,-1,-i,1,i,-1,-i,\ldots 1,-i,-1,i,1,-i,-1,i,\ldots And these are just what we need. We have four sequences and four constraints to satisfy (we want the period to be (1,0,0,0) ), so we can do it. In fact it’s very simple: just adding together all of those Fourier sequences gives us that pulse train, times 4 : 4(1,0,0,0)=(1,1,1,1)+(1,i,-1,-i)+(1,-1,1,-1)+(1,-i,-1,i) Therefore, expanding (1+1)^n , (1+i)^n , (1-1)^n and (1-i)^n produces four weighted sums of binomial coefficients which, when added together, conspire to interfere with each other just right to leave every fourth binomial coefficient intact and eliminate everything else. In other words, whatever n is, \displaystyle 4\sum_{k=0}^\infty \binom{n}{4k}=(1+1)^n+(1+i)^n+(1-1)^n+(1-i)^n=2^n+(1+i)^n(1+(-i)^n) (In the last equality we simply replace 1-i with -i(1+i) and collect like terms.) Oh, that’s great: when n=34 , or more generally when n\equiv 2\pmod 4 , the last term vanishes, and we find \displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^\infty \binom{n}{4k}=2^{n-2} So the answer to the question is simply 2^{32} . (I wrote the sum extending all the way to infinity, as in the question, but this is just to save a more cumbersome upper limit. The binomial coefficients simply vanish when 4k exceeds n .) Without too much trouble we can write down simple formulas for those binomial sums for all other values of n . Furthermore, using that same method we can handle sums of binomial coefficients like \sum_k \binom{n}{4k+1} , and generally \sum_k\binom{n}{dk+e} , and… …In fact, if you generalize what we just did, you’ll discover a wildly strong technique. We had a sequence of numbers a_0,a_1,a_2,\ldots which we understood well enough to recognize its generating function f(X)=a_0+a_1X+a_2X^2+\ldots We needed to calculate a sum of a “sampled” version of the sequence, and the way we did that was to express the sampling map 1,0,0,0,1,0,0,0,1,0,0,0,\ldots (or any other sampling or weighting) as a linear combination of powers of a root of unity, which is simply the discrete Fourier transform. With that, we are able to express the sampled sum as a linear combination of various values f(\omega^m) , where \omega is the appropriate root of unity. The very same idea (in a multiplicative, rather than additive, context) was used by Dirichlet to estimate the number of primes in arithmetic progressions, and started an enormous and fruitful thread of ideas in mathematics. I love how this little problem pushes us in this magnificent direction. (Added later) A bijective proof The solution above is instructive, since the technique is so general. But whenever such an elegant identity shows up, one must wonder why it’s true – what is a combinatorial explanation? We’ve discovered that, when n is divisible by 4 , \displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^\infty \binom{n+2}{4k} = 2^n \tag 4 On the left we are counting sequences of 0 ’s and 1 ’s of length n+2 where the number of 1 's is a multiple of 4 , and on the right we are counting sequences of 0 's and 1 's of length n with no further constraint. Why do these two sets have the same size? There ought to be a natural bijection between them. And indeed there is. Here’s the one I managed to find after posting this answer. There may be other, better ones. Given any bit-string S of length n having k 1 's, we can augment it to a bit-string of length n+2 with the appropriate number of 1 's, as follows: If k \equiv 0 \pmod 4 , attach 00 at the end of S . If k \equiv 2 \pmod 4 , attach 11 at the end of S . If k \equiv 3 \pmod 4 , attach 01 at the end of S . If k \equiv 1 \pmod 4 , flip all the bits of S (replace each 0 by a 1 and vice versa), and then attach 10 at the end of S . In the first three cases it is obvious that the number of 1 's in the augmented string is divisible by 4 : we added just the necessary number of 1 's. In the last case, we couldn’t fix the number of 1 's simply by attaching two bits, since there are three missing 1 's. So we first flip all the bits in S , changing the number of 1 's from k to n-k , and this is where it’s important that n is divisible by 4 : the number of 1 's now is 3 mod 4 , and we can once again fix it by adding one 1 . We do this by attaching 10 instead of 01 , which lets us know which strings were flipped and which weren’t. That’s important, because this is why we get a bijection . Given a long string with n+2 bits, we can reconstruct the original S : remove the last two bits, and flip the result if those last two bits were 10 . This is known as a bijective proof. It shows why the equation (4) is true by explicitly pairing up elements in two sets whose number of elements are the LHS and the RHS of the equation. More things I should have said The result we’ve obtained expresses the unknown magnitude as a combination (1+1)^n+(1-1)^n+(1+i)^n+(1-i)^n One of these is, of course, 0 , but it’s a little surprising that the last two cancel out. This is actually a very deep and very general phenomenon. When such expressions come up, there’s often a leading term coming from the trivial Fourier coefficient, which is the 2^n here. The other terms tend to interfere with each other destructively. They don’t always cancel so cleanly, but when they don’t, they leave an “error term” which is much smaller than the leading term. For example, let’s go back to the equation \displaystyle 4\sum_{k=0}^\infty \binom{n}{4k}=2^n+(1+i)^n(1+(-i)^n) If n is divisible by 4 , let us write n=4m . We now have (1+(-i)^n)=2 , and since (1+i)^4=-4 , (1+i)^{4m}=(-2)^{2m} , so we get (after dividing by 4 ): \displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^\infty \binom{4m}{4k}=2^{4m-2}+(-2)^{2m-1} so there is a correction term now, but it’s like the square root of the leading term – much smaller. This is very typical of those interference/filtration/Fourier results. Finally, test your understanding! Find a nice, explicit expression for the following infinite sum without any calculator (or even pen and paper): \displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{1}{(4n)!} .
what-do-complex-numbers-mean-physically: What do complex numbers mean physically? — Doesn’t work like that. Let’s start with real numbers. What do they mean physically? Well, everything and nothing. Everything, because we use real numbers as models for position, distance, time, mass, temperature, energy, momentum, current and plenty of other things. Nothing, because none of these things is actually represented by a real number – we have no idea what goes on below a certain scale, and using real numbers as a model is just convenient. Similarly, complex numbers don’t mean anything physically. We can choose to use complex numbers to model various things that nicely fit their behavior. For example, the impedance of certain electrical components like capacitors and inductors can conveniently be modeled with complex numbers, because their effect on periodic currents changes both magnitude and phases. Is current, or impedance, “really” what a complex number is, or what it physically means? Not at all. Complex numbers are an idea which is decoupled from the physical world. But they can be used to model certain physical phenomena, like this one. More importantly, complex numbers provide the basic framework for quantum mechanics – states, wave functions and so on. The way quantum mechanical systems evolve and interact with each other relies heavily on the algebra of complex numbers. And still, it’s incorrect to say that the field of scalars of quantum theories is what complex numbers “mean”. They happen to be very suitable for that task, and a whole host of others, inside or outside the physical world.
can-there-exist-100-lines-in-the-plane-n: Can there exist 100 lines in the plane, no three concurrent, such that they intersect in exactly 2002 points? — Yup. This looks like a geometry problem, right? It’s not. It’s a problem in number theory. The geometry part is almost entirely a red herring. You see, when you have lines in the plane, any two lines intersect either once or not at all, with “not at all” happening exactly when they are parallel. The number of meeting points is, therefore, just the number of pairs of non-parallel lines. Oh, may we be double-counting points where multiple lines meet? No worries, this isn’t occurring here: we are told that no three lines are concurrent. Every meeting point is on just two lines. So, the actual arrangement of the lines in the plane is immaterial. The only thing that matters is how they are grouped into batches of parallel lines (called “pencils”). Other than this, how the lines are oriented and the distances between them make no difference whatsoever. If we only had six lines, we could (for example) arrange them as three pencils: three parallel ones, another parallel pair in a different direction, and a single line not parallel to either of those. We would then have 11 meeting points: 3\times 2+3\times 1+2\times 1 . (Pencils of 3, 2 and 1 lines yield 11 intersections). Observe how, once the grey and blue pencils are in place, it doesn’t matter at all where the orange line is placed. It just needs to have a new direction, and not to pass through any of the existing intersections. Wherever it is, there will be exactly 11 intersections. In our case, we need to group our lines into pencils of unknown sizes a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_k . The total number of lines in the pencils is 100=a_1+\ldots+a_k , and the number of intersection points needs to be 2002=P=\sum_{i<j} a_i a_j . The number of variables, k , is also up to us. The question is, therefore, can we come up with such positive integers? If we can solve this diophantine question, we can solve the problem just by laying down pencils of the required magnitudes. If the diophantine question has no solution, the arrangement of lines cannot exist. So: are there positive integers which add up to 100 and whose pairwise products add up to 2002 ? To answer this, I made a small algebraic change. The pairwise sum is reminiscent of the formula for the squared sum (a_1+\ldots+a_k)^2 . Indeed, \displaystyle (a_1+\ldots+a_k)^2=S+2P Where S=\sum a_i^2 is the sum of squares and P is the sum of pairwise products. We know that this is 100^2 , so the sum of squares S must be 100^2-2\times 2002=5996 . Our diophantine question has changed to finding positive integers a_1,\ldots,a_k whose sum is 100 and whose sum of squares is 5996 . My first assumption was that such numbers do not exist, but I couldn’t see why. The parity works fine, the magnitude is reasonable, and I’m still curious if there is a good set of criteria for checking if a sum of squares is feasible given the sum. At any rate, this isn’t an issue here. At some point I decided to just go greedy and write 5996 as a sum of squares of numbers which add up to 100 . By “greedy” I meant to start with the largest square I can and go from there. I was in the theater while solving this. My son is playing Samuel in the local youth theater’s performance of Pirates of Penzance , and when he wasn’t on stage I indulged in a bit of calculating. I figured that 76^2=5776 is the largest square smaller than 5996 , which is incorrect, but I hadn’t noticed. I was happy to see that the difference is 220 and the remainder to 100 is 24 , which seemed like nice numbers, so I stuck with them. Now I had to make 220 a sum of squares of numbers which add up to 24 . Being greedy once again (this time correctly) I started with 14^2=196 , leaving 24 for the sum of squares and 10 for the sum. I went with 4^2=16 , and it was plain sailing from here. So, the numbers (76,14,4,2,1,1,1,1) have sum 100 and sum of squares 5996 , just like we need. The problem is solved, in the positive: make 76 parallel lines in some direction, 14 other parallel lines in another direction, then 4 , then 2 , and then four individual lines in four random directions not parallel to anything else. The number of intersection points is going to be 2002 . Had I been more careful, I would have noticed that 77^2<5996 , so we can try writing the difference 67 as a sum of squares of numbers adding up to 23 . Greedily taking 7^2=49 as our next number leaves us with square-sum 18 and sum 16 . You do not want to be greedy now: taking 4^2=16 leaves you with too many leftover numbers. Instead, just take 14 1 's and a single 2 . So another solution is (77,7,2,1,\ldots,1) with fourteen 1 's. There are many other solutions.
why-are-there-so-many-intellectuals-e-g-: Why are there so many intellectuals (e.g. those in certain branches of mathematics and philosophy) thinking so hard about problems whose solutions have little to no real-world significance? Are all truths actually profound and important to arrive at? — The reason people think hard about problems that interest them is because the problems interest them. They don’t know if the solutions have “little to no real-world significance” (and neither do you), and they don’t care. They profoundly enjoy the journey, the learnings, and the creative process. Most enjoyable human endeavors have “little to no real-world significance”. People climb mountains, play music, go to the beach, read, have sex, travel, keep flower gardens and study 16th-century poetry because we are curious creatures and voracious seekers of sublime joy. In case what you really mean to ask is why we, as a society, allow people to pursue such fun activities instead of ensuring that everyone constantly contributes to what you deem to have real-world significance, well, we tried that too. Didn’t end very well. In case what you really mean to ask is why we, as a society, choose to go even further and financially support such intellectual pursuits as the research of abstract mathematical problems with no real-life deliverables or real-world significance, well, there are several good reasons. One, it’s incredibly cheap. Two, research mathematicians have proven to be amazingly effective teachers, partners and collaborators to engineers, chemists, physicists, economists, biologists, software engineers and many other practitioners of real life. Three, math turns out to be very useful, even pieces of it that were once considered not useful. Inventors thrive in intellectual communities that span the practical and the abstract. Applied mathematicians thrive when surrounded by engineers and pure mathematicians. Students young and old are inspired by the dramatic discoveries, proofs and towers of abstraction which permeate the world of mathematics. If you ever start a nation or design a country, I would warmly encourage you not to limit the spectrum of allowed vocations to what you regard as immediately beneficial and practical. Leave some room for poetry, fashion design and abstract math. Your world will be incredibly better for them.
introductory-courses-in-linear-algebra-t: Introductory courses in linear algebra tend to start with either vectors or systems of equations. Which do you prefer to start your course with and why? — “Hello everyone! This is an introductory course in Linear Algebra. Linear Algebra is absolutely fundamental for both the theory and application of mathematics, and it provides an excellent opportunity for us to experience the power and beauty of the abstract approach . The main actors in Linear Algebra are vector spaces and linear transformations. Vector spaces arise whenever you have things which you can add and scale, and linear transformations are those transformations that respect adding and scaling. I know this sounds very abstract, and we will of course make it precise and clear. What I want us to understand first, though, is why this abstraction is a good thing. You see, it’s possible to go through an entire Linear Algebra course and talk about just one type of vectors, usually “tuples” of real numbers such as (23,-6.41,\pi,19) . There’s still a lot of techniques and algorithms to learn, and this can be useful for many practical purposes. But it’s missing out on a fantastic opportunity to widen our horizons and make this course mean so much more. When you work with the abstract definitions, you invest just a little bit additional effort, and get a thousandfold more in return. Bit strings used in communication and encryption are vectors. Solutions of differential equations are vectors. Quantum states in physics are vectors. Computer images are vectors. Elements of field extensions are vectors. Points in space are vectors. Forces and velocities and electric fields are vectors. Lots and lots of different things are vectors, vector spaces, linear transformations, eigenvalues and so on. To make any of these work, you must free yourself from thinking that vectors are a bunch of numbers and the only thing you can do with them is multiply them by matrices. You need vector spaces over finite fields, you need infinite dimensional vector spaces, you need to see that laplacians and gradients and Fourier transforms are linear transformations. Then you see why Linear Algebra is so important. Furthermore, the whole idea of “abstract approach”, of defining entities using axioms and exploring them with observations and proofs, is a tremendously valuable intellectual challenge which is in some ways more important than Linear Algebra itself. This is how real math is done, and at some point you’re going to learn it, and now is a really good time to do it, in the context of Linear Algebra. So, that’s what we are going to do. We will learn to handle abstract definitions, we will learn to read and create and write proofs, we will learn about fields and vectors and linear transformations and eigenvalues in their most general and wide-ranging manifestations – and we will also learn a few techniques for solving equations and diagonalizing matrices, because the practice of Linear Algebra is important as well. So, shall we begin?” ( Me, addressing the classroom, imaginary universe #17 .)
can-you-show-me-how-to-integrate-by-usin: Can you show me how to integrate by using partial fractions? — Oh, I’d be happy to. Integration by partial fractions has a peculiar pedagogical pedigree. It is often presented in calculus courses as a way of integrating rational functions, but it is rarely accompanied by a complete theoretical description – it’s more like a messy recipe with various cases which suffice for the final exam. The presentation leaves many students unsure what exactly is it that they’re doing, what the general case is like, and why. This is usually left unresolved throughout undergrad and graduate studies. I can’t think of another instance where a basic result or technique is taught in such a half-assed way. Curriculum designers often choose to leave or include this or that in an undergrad program, but when something is included, it is usually included properly. The situation with partial fractions is akin to learning about the Jordan canonical form in the real case only, and merely through a few examples. It’s a travesty. In the paper by Bradley and Cook I cite below, they write: Analysts view this as pure algebra (which it is) so it should not be addressed in a course on analysis. Algebraists typically view partial fractions as a technique only good for integrating and thus a problem for analysts. So, outside of the realm of symbolic computation, the partial fraction decomposition tends to never be fully discussed. This doesn’t bother all students, perhaps not even most students, but it drives people like me insane. I can’t comprehend anything if I don’t see the general context and complete proofs. Scattered techniques like this make me feel like my knowledge has decreased, rather than increased. So, here’s my attempt at addressing this. I’ll try to explain the idea behind partial fraction decomposition in various contexts, as well as its (very legitimate) connection to integration, and perhaps a few other uses if we have time. I can’t do the topic full justice in an answer; I will merely be able to outline how I would teach this if I were to. Shall we? Representations Everyone knows that natural numbers can be written down as usual, in decimal notation, like 196884 , or through their prime factorization, as in 2^2 \times 3^3 \times 1823 . Most people (I think) also understand that various things are easier or harder to do in either form of notation. Many students of math also know that something very similar is true of polynomials. A (single variable) polynomial can be written down as x^8 + 2 x^7 - 2 x^6 - 6 x^5 + 6 x^3 + 2 x^2 - 2 x - 1 , a sum of powers of x with coefficients, or as a product of irreducible factors with possible multiplicity, as in (x^2+1)^2(x-1)^2 . Once again, certain tasks become easier with either form of presentation. Now, what about rational numbers? And what about rational functions, which are the analogous thing for polynomials? We usually write rational numbers like \frac{77}{12} : a numerator and a denominator expressed as decimals. Of course we can factor both numbers and write \frac{7 \times 11}{2^2 \times 3} . Same thing. But there are other ways. One form is a continued fraction, as in \displaystyle \frac{77}{12} = 6+\frac{1}{2+\frac{1}{2+\frac{1}{2}}} This is also (extremely) useful in various ways, but we won’t go there now. Are there other ways? Well, yes there are. For reasons which, I think, aren’t fully understood, early texts from Egypt’s Middle Kingdom exhibit a strong preference to represent fractions as sums of distinct unit fractions, as in \displaystyle \frac{29}{24} = \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{8} . Such representations, dubbed “ Egyptian Fractions ”, do sometimes have a utility, but they aren’t important enough nowadays to be taught as a systematic way of representing rational numbers. We should note the idea, though: we are decomposing a rational number into a sum of fractions which have a certain simplicity. They all have a numerator of 1 . Also, let’s note something about the denominators in that representations: 2, 3, 4 and 8 all divide 24 . This isn’t surprising, when you think about what happens when you add up fractions. We’ll see how this plays out later. What would be the analogous thing for rational functions? And why would it be useful? Integrating Rational Functions First, a reminder: a rational function is a ratio of two polynomials, such as \displaystyle \frac{x^5-2x^3+1}{x^2-3} . In general, we write \displaystyle R(x) = \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} where f,g are polynomials. Rational functions come up in many different contexts, both in pure math and in applications. Just like rational numbers, they can be represented in different ways, so first let us motivate why we would go looking for a representation as a sum of simple fractions. When we learn about derivatives, we quickly see that differentiating any expression is a purely mechanical process. This is because, once we know to differentiate f and g , we can also handle f+g , fg , and also f \circ g which is the composition f(g(x)) . Then we start going the other way, finding anti derivatives: given a function f , we seek a function F with F'=f . This is usually denoted as F=\int f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x , an indefinite integral. And here things get complicated. Indefinite integrals are linear, so they behave nicely with respect to addition and scalar multiplication. But unfortunately, that’s pretty much it. If you know the antiderivatives of f and g , there’s generally no way to determine the antiderivatives of fg or f\circ g and so on. We do know how to integrate polynomials, and even some very simple rational functions, because we all know that \frac{d}{dx}x^n = nx^{n-1} , and so \displaystyle \int x^k \,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{1}{k+1}x^{k+1} for any integer k \ne -1 , while \displaystyle \int x^{-1} \,\mathrm{d}x = \log(x) where \log denotes the natural logarithm. As a result, we can also handle \int (x-a)^k\,\mathrm{d}x for any number a and integer k . Ok great. But what about more complicated rational functions, like \frac{x^3+x+5}{x^2-1} ? Well, obviously , all we need to do is manage to write every rational function as a sum of those simple ones, like \frac{1}{(x-a)^k} , or even \frac{17}{(x-a)^k} , since we aren’t worried about multiplicative constants. Integrating sums is easy, even with whatever multiplicative constants (aka linear combinations). Note well: the “simple” fractions we seek have very simple numerators, just numbers; and denominators which are just powers of a linear polynomial. As we shall see, this works perfect over the complex numbers, but another complication is introduced if we insist on working with real numbers only. Partial Fraction Decomposition: Fooling Around Before we do the general case, let’s look at some simple examples. \displaystyle \frac{1}{x-1} This one is already fine. We know how to integrate (x-1)^{-1} . \displaystyle \frac{x}{x-1} Notice how merely changing the numerator from 1 to x makes the integral non-obvious. However, there’s an easy fix: \displaystyle \frac{x}{x-1} = \frac{x-1+1}{x-1}=1+\frac{1}{x-1} and similarly \displaystyle \frac{x^2}{x-1} = \frac{(x+1)(x-1)+1}{x-1} =(x+1)+\frac{1}{x-1} what’s going on here? This should remind you of something: we’re simply replacing the numerator with a quotient and remainder upon division by the denominator. \displaystyle \frac{19}{6} = \frac{3 \times 6 + 1}{6} = 3+\frac{1}{6} In a similar way, we re-wrote the numerator x^2 as q(x)(x-1)+r(x) , a quotient and a remainder. A basic skill you should have before tackling partial fractions is polynomial division with remainder, aka the Euclidean Algorithm for polynomials. It really works the exact same way as with numbers. The general conclusion here is that we can handle anything of the form \displaystyle \frac{f(x)}{x-1} by simply dividing f(x) = q(x)(x-1)+r(x) , and so \displaystyle \frac{f(x)}{x-1} = q(x)+\frac{r(x)}{x-1} In fact, since the denominator has degree 1 , the remainder r(x) is guaranteed to simply be a constant – just a number. We have no trouble integrating this. Ok, let’s move on. \displaystyle \frac{1}{(x-1)^2} Still no problem. This is (x-1)^{-2} . Easy to integrate. \displaystyle \frac{x}{(x-1)^2} Hmmm. Polynomial division won’t save us here, because the numerator already had a smaller degree than the denominator. What do we do? Here comes one of the basic ideas of Partial Fraction Decomposition. We can’t possibly hope to rewrite \frac{x}{(x-1)^2} as simply \frac{a}{(x-1)^2} for some number a , because x isn’t a constant. But we might still hope to manage something like this: \displaystyle \frac{x}{(x-1)^2} = \frac{a}{x-1}+\frac{b}{(x-1)^2} Why is that reasonable? Well, adding together the fractions on the right, we find \displaystyle \frac{a}{x-1}+\frac{b}{(x-1)^2} = \frac{a(x-1)+b}{(x-1)^2} The denominator is simply (x-1)^2 , which is what we need, and the numerator looks darn close to a general polynomial of the first degree. Great: we can surely adjust a and b so they make a(x-1)+b be whatever we want, such as our original numerator which happened to be x . Clearly we want a=1 , and then we get (x-1)+b , so we want b=1 as well. \displaystyle \frac{x}{(x-1)^2} = \frac{1}{x-1}+\frac{1}{(x-1)^2} The cool thing is, we could have done the exact same thing with \frac{mx+n}{(x-1)^2} for any numbers m,n . We just need to match a(x-1)+b with mx+n , which is no trouble at all. And the coolest thing is, this lets us handle numerators up to degree 1 , and numerators of degree 2 and beyond can be handled as before, by first dividing by the denominator, being left with a remainder of lower degree – meaning, the first degree! We are able to exactly match the freedom we need. You may guess how this is going to go from here. For things like \frac{f(x)}{(x-1)^3} , we will first reduce f(x) to a remainder of the second degree, and then handle it by finding appropriate constants a,b,c to make \frac{a}{x-1}+\frac{b}{(x-1)^2}+\frac{c}{(x-1)^3} do what we need it to do. Ok. So far the denominators were all (x-1)^k for some power k . The same thing obviously works for (x-u)^k for any u , but what about more complicated denominators? For example, what are we supposed to do with \displaystyle \frac{1}{x^2-1} ? Well, x^2-1 factors as (x-1)(x+1) . Does this help? Can we hope to achieve \displaystyle \frac{1}{x^2-1} = \frac{a}{x-1}+\frac{b}{x+1} ? Why, sure. Again, let’s just add up those guys on the right, getting \frac{a(x+1)+b(x-1)}{(x-1)(x+1)} . The numerator can be adjusted to be any linear polynomial, and that’s all we need since the denominator has degree 2 . What’s the general lesson? The general lesson is that the denominator g(x) should be broken down into a product of (x-u) 's, and then we rewrite the fraction as a sum of simple things over these (x-u) 's individually. We’ve also learned that if any (x-u) appears with multiplicity, as in (x-u)^k , we should allow for denominators of (x-u)^j for j=1,2,\ldots,k , to get enough freedom to match our numerators. Partial Fractions over the Complex Numbers But… can we factor any polynomial g(x) into linear factors, as in g(x)=(x-u)^k(x-v)^l\ldots(x-w)^m ? Can we? Well, sure we can. That’s just what complex numbers were made for. Over the complex numbers, any polynomial has just as many roots as its degree, or in other words, every polynomial factors completely into linear factors. Therefore, over the complex numbers, the random meanderings we just went through are completely sufficient to achieve a partial fraction decomposition of any rational function. It can have rational coefficients, it can have real coefficients, it can even have complex coefficients, doesn’t matter – it’s totally doable. Start with \displaystyle R(x) = \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} If the degree of f(x) is greater than that of g(x) , use long division to write f(x) = q(x)g(x)+r(x) where r has lower degree. Then \displaystyle R(x) = q(x) + \frac{r(x)}{g(x)} and now the numerator r(x) is smaller, in terms of degree, than the denominator. Next, factor g(x) = (x-u_1)(x-u_2)\cdots(x-u_n) . The roots u_1,u_2,\ldots,u_n may not be distinct, so a better way to write this is \displaystyle g(x) = (x-u_1)^{m_1}\cdots(x-u_k)^{m_k} where u_1,\ldots,u_k are the distinct roots and m_1,\ldots,m_k are their multiplicities. We expect to need simple fractions that look like \frac{a_{ij}}{(x-u_i)^j} where a_{ij} are just some numbers, nothing fancy, and the denominators are all powers of (x-u_i) , never exceeding the appropriate multiplicity, meaning j =1,2,\ldots,m_i . So the overall decomposition we expect looks like this: \displaystyle \frac{r(x)}{g(x)} = \sum_{i=1}^k \sum_{j=1}^{m_i} \frac{a_{ij}}{(x-u_i)^j} This looks a bit scary, but seriously, it’s nothing. You merely write out the right hand side, add things up, and solve for the a_{ij} to make them fit your actual numerator r(x) . It’s nothing worse than solving linear equations, and you are guaranteed to succeed since there are just enough parameters a_{ij} to fit the numerator r(x) . A formal proof of this can be written down in several ways. Since this answer is long enough as it is, let me point you to a wonderful paper by Bradley and Cook (from, incredibly, 2012!), which does everything with complete rigor. This Just Isn’t Hard Enough: Real Numbers The way partial fractions are taught in most calculus or real analysis classes involves one more layer of complication, because teachers often insist on doing everything with real numbers. Honestly, in my mind, this adds unnecessary stress on top of something which is already notationally cumbersome, even if it’s not really complicated. Complex numbers are just awesome in how they let you factor any polynomial down to linear factors – why not use them? Here’s what actually happens in the classroom. Using the general method we just outlined, we find \displaystyle \frac{1}{x^2-1} = \frac{1/2}{x-1}-\frac{1/2}{x+1} so we can integrate \frac{1}{x^2-1} easily using logs. \displaystyle \int \frac{1}{x^2-1}\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{1}{2}\log(x-1)-\frac{1}{2}\log(x+1) . Similarly, \displaystyle \frac{1}{x^2+1} = \frac{-i/2}{x-i}+\frac{i/2}{x+i} so \displaystyle \int \frac{1}{x^2+1}\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{i}{2}\log(x+i)-\frac{i}{2}\log(x-i) but that’s not the answer most teachers want, unfortunately. They want \text{arctan}(x) or \text{atan}(x) or \tan^{-1}(x) or whatever they call the inverse tangent function. Now of course, it’s the same thing . The expression we just wrote down with logs and i is exactly the inverse tangent. An antiderivative is an antiderivative; there can’t be two of them, except for additive constants. But we’re supposed to fear the complex number, so instead of doing it the right and easy way, we complicate things more. Remember: partial fraction decomposition is really quite straightforward with complex numbers. You factor the denominator completely, you write down the required denominators to cover the multiplicities, done. Integrating is never more complicated then knowing how to integrate (x-u)^k , which is really easy. But if you insist on doing things with real numbers only, you still can… at a cost. A polynomial with real coefficients cannot always be factored into linear factors with real coefficients, but it can factored into linear and quadratic factors with real coefficients. (Why? Because the complex non-real roots of a real polynomial must come in conjugate pairs, and multiplying these pairs out gives you real quadratics). That’s not the end of the world. It just means that now, even in the absence of those annoying multiplicities, we will need to allow terms such as \displaystyle \frac{ax+b}{x^2+ux+v} in our partial fraction decomposition. If we also have multiplicities, we will likewise need to allow \displaystyle \frac{ax+b}{x^2+ux+v}+\frac{cx+d}{(x^2+ux+v)^2} or additional terms like this if the multiplicity is higher. The process of figuring out the coefficients now becomes correspondingly more cumbersome, but this is really just a nuisance. In terms of integration, it also means that we need to know how to integrate those simple fractions: linear numerators and quadratic denominators. This isn’t hard either, using a few standard trigonometric integrals. The general philosophy of partial fraction decomposition for rational functions over the real numbers is still the same: we write a general rational function as a sum of a polynomial and simple fractions, where “simple” now means having powers of linear of quadratic terms in the denominators, and nothing worse than linear polynomials in the numerators. Since we know how to integrate those, we can integrate any rational function. The General Case It is tempting to try and generalize everything we just did. We’ve handled rational functions over the real and complex numbers; what about other fields? And what if, instead of polynomials, we look at fractions made of elements of other rings? One of the simplest steps in our process was the reduction of the numerator into something of lower degree than the denominator. This concept of “degree” generalizes nicely into something called Euclidean domains, where you have a “degree” function and a guaranteed division with a remainder which has smaller degree than what you’re dividing by. In the general case, we cannot hope to control the degree of the irreducible factors of the denominators. Above, we made good use of the fact that complex numbers guarantee linear factors only, and real numbers guarantee linear or quadratic ones. In general, we don’t have a limit on the degrees of the irreducible factors, but that’s ok: we can still achieve a partial fraction decomposition where the denominators are powers of irreducible factors. This helps clarify things, I think. The denominators in the approach as it’s usually taught are a hodge-podge of linear and quadratic factors with various powers. The underlying mechanism is irreducibility : you factor the denominator as much as you can, and allow for power of these factors in the decomposition. One interesting quirk is that, in those more general cases, the decomposition ends up being non-unique. There doesn’t seem to be a simple recipe to define precisely the conditions on the terms that would guarantee uniqueness. The decomposition always exists , but it’s not necessarily unique in any obvious sense. For the purposes of finding antiderivatives, this really isn’t a concern at all. The decomposition we’ve described over \C and \R is, in fact, unique, but it doesn’t really need to be: we know from other considerations that an antiderivative must be unique up to an additive constant (since f'=g' implies (f-g)'=0 , so f-g is a constant). But it’s an interesting observation nonetheless. Uniqueness is often harder than mere existence, and it’s equally often very much necessary. To go back to the context we started with, way back at the top of this answer: what can we say about the partial fraction decomposition of ordinary rational numbers? Well, it does always exist, and it is actually unique if we insist on always taking positive remainders. We get things like \frac{77}{12}=5+\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2^2}+\frac{2}{3} note that this isn’t the “Egyptian Fraction” decomposition from ancient Egypt, but we do see how the numerators are smaller than the denominators. Also observe how we subtly needed to reduce the integer part from 6 to 5 in order for the decomposition to work. It’s a fascinating way of representing rational numbers, but unfortunately it’s not particularly useful (as far as we know), so we never teach it, which leaves the calculus technique sort of hanging there without context or precedent, which is really a shame. It’s a simple, and very useful, technique.
what-are-some-examples-of-non-trivial-or: What are some examples of non-trivial or difficult counterexamples to mathematical conjectures? — Oh, this is going to be fun. First, a point of terminology: there are no “counterexamples to mathematical theories ”, because a theory isn’t a single statement that can be refuted with a counterexample. Nor are there counterexamples to mathematical theorems , because theorems are true. There do exist interesting, non-trivial and sometimes complicated counterexamples to mathematical statements which, of course, aren’t theorems. Many of those statements have stood as conjectures for a while, until someone found a counterexample. Some of the following counterexamples are profound, some mundane. Some are easy to verify, some aren’t. Some are in Number Theory, some in the Theory of Computation, some in Logic and some in Topology (and maybe a few other fields, we’ll see). Claim : Every number of the form 2^{2^n}+1 is prime. (False!) This was a genuine conjecture made by Pierre de Fermat, who verified that 2^2+1=5 , 2^4+1=17 , 2^8+1=257 and 2^{16}+1=65537 are indeed primes. The counterexample comes precisely at the next number, 2^{32}+1=4294967297=641 \times 6700417 . This may seem trivial by today’s standards, but when Euler found this factorization it was quite a clever feat (he did this by recognizing that 641=2^9+2^7+1 must divide that number). In fact, Fermat was about as wrong about this as can be: as far as we can tell, past n\geq 5 none of the numbers 2^{2^n}+1 is prime. We don’t know this for sure, though. We know that 2^{2^{32}}+1 is composite (as are all smaller numbers of this form), but nobody knows for sure if 2^{2^{33}}+1 is or isn’t prime. Claim (Tait’s Conjecture) : Every planar, 3-connected cubic graph has a Hamiltonian cycle. (False!) This was proposed in 1884 by P. G. Tait as a way to prove the famous 4-Color Theorem: Tait showed (quite easily) that the 4-color theorem follows from this statement. It took more than 60 years for Bill Tutte to find this counterexample: This graph is obviously planar, it is obviously cubic (every vertex has exactly three neighbors), it is slightly less obviously 3-connected (it cannot be separated by removing one or two vertices), and it’s not Hamiltonian (there’s no way to visit all the vertices in one continuous path with no loops). This last part isn’t at all obvious but it’s not super difficult to prove, either. It’s finding this graph that’s the challenge. Claim : If you add up some k th powers to get a k th power, you must have added at least k numbers. (False!) This conjecture was made by none other than Leonhard Euler, as a certain extension of Fermat’s Last Theorem. Euler observed that it’s easy to add up two squares to get a square, as in 3^2+4^2=5^2 , but you can’t add two cubes to get a cube: a^3+b^3=c^3 has no solution in positive integers (This is the case n=3 of Fermat’s Last Theorem, which Euler was the first to actually prove.) You can , however, add up three cubes to get a cube, for example 3^3+4^3+5^3=6^3 . Well, thought Euler, there’s a pattern here: you can add up k k th powers to get a k th power, but you can’t get away with fewer than k of them. This isn’t true, but it took almost 200 years to find a counterexample. The first counterexample was found in 1966 by Lander and Parkin, using a computer search. They discovered that 27^5+84^5+110^5+133^5=144^5 . You can find their original paper here . In 1966, this was quite a feat. Nowadays, you can find this example in just a few minutes of coding and running your code on a standard laptop, or even a smartphone (Try it!). This shows that Euler was wrong when k=5 . He already knew that he was right for k=3 . What about k=4 ? That took considerably more ingenuity than a mere computer search. In 1986, 20-year-old Noam Elkies used the theory of elliptic curves (plus some computer work) to find infinitely many counterexamples to Euler’s conjecture for fourth powers. The smallest one is 2682440^4+15365639^4+18796760^4=20615673^4 . Finally, for k \geq 6 , the situation is still unknown. It is possible, though in my mind unlikely, that Euler’s conjecture holds for 6th powers and beyond. We aren’t quite done with Euler, though. Claim : There are no Orthogonal Squares of even order which is not divisible by 4 . (False!) Look at the following array of cards. A♠ K♥ Q♦ J♣ Q♣ J♦ A♥ K♠ J♥ Q♠ K♣ A♦ K♦ A♣ J♠ Q♥ See how clever this is: every row contains each rank (J, Q, K, A) exactly once, as does each column. Also, every row contains each suit (♠,♥,♦,♣) exactly once, as does each column. But moreover, the two arrangements of rank and suits are so mixed up that no card appears twice in the entire array: the Jack of Hearts appears just once, as does the Queen of Spades, and so on for all possible combinations. Without this last “orthogonality” condition, what you’d have here is just two superimposed Sudoku puzzles of order 4. But the requirement to have none of the pairs appear twice makes it a very hard puzzle, hard enough to interest the great Euler. He used latin and greek letters to build those arrays, earning them then name Graeco-Latin square. Here’s such an array of order 3. Euler was able to construct such arrays for every odd order and for every order divisible by 4. It’s easy to see that there’s no such array for order 2 (exercise!), and Euler was unable to build one of order 6, so he proposed that the orders 2, 6, 10, 14, … are impossible. Those are the even numbers that aren’t divisible by 4. Euler was wrong about that, too, and once again it took more than 150 years for this conjecture to be refuted (at this point I should probably mention that Euler was one of the most profound and creative mathematicians of all time, and those conjectural snafus were quite uncharacteristic of him.) Euler was right about order 6, though it was only in 1901 that this was proven. But in 1959, Raj Chandra Bose and Sharadchandra Shankar Shrikhande constructed an orthogonal array of order 22. E. T. Parker found an example of order 10, and later the three of them proved that such arrays exist for every n except the gaps at n=2 and n=6 . Here’s an orthogonal array of order 10: every 2-digit combination appears exactly once, and every row and every column contain every digit in both the first and second places. Claim : There are no Turing degrees between 0 and 0′ . (False)! The theory of Turing degrees is a truly beautiful idea. It studies the computational aspects of sets of numbers, and reveals an amazingly intricate structure from a few simple definitions. Here are the minimum basics we need. A set of natural numbers is called computable if you can write a computer program that checks for membership in the set. Since you can write a computer program that checks if a number is prime, the set of primes is computable. Since you can write a computer program that checks if a given number is even and is the sum of two primes, the set of even numbers which are the sum of two primes is computable (We don’t know if this set contains all even numbers greater than 2, which is Goldbach’s conjecture; but the set is nevertheless computable). The family of all computable sets is called 0 . Not every set of natural numbers is computable, because there are far too many sets and far too few possible computer programs to detect them. As a concrete example of a non-computable set, consider the set of numbers which encode (in some way) computer programs which halt. No computer program can correctly determine if a number is or isn’t in the set . Now, suppose you are given a magical gadget which can , actually, tell you if a program halts or not. Using this gadget as “black box” (or, in more common parlance, an “oracle”), you can now do better and write computer programs that decide membership in more sets than just the computable ones. Those sets are said to be “computable using a halting oracle”, and the family of those sets is denoted 0′ . It also carries the captivating name “The Turing jump of 0 ”. Emil Post asked the question: are there sets that are harder to verify than 0 but easier to verify than 0′ ? A bit more formally, is there a set which is not computable but is computable with a halting oracle, and which is itself not powerful enough to serve as a halting oracle? It seems a bit hard to imagine that such intermediate-level problems exist. But they do. Richard Friedberg and Albert Muchnik, independently, developed the idea known as the Priority Method and constructed such peculiar sets. This opened a whole new field of study, exploring the rich structure of Turing degrees and their partial order. Claim : There are no models of ZFC which violate the Continuum Hypothesis . (False!) Georg Cantor, the creator of the Theory of Sets, wondered if there’s an uncountable set of real numbers which cannot be put in correspondence with the real numbers. In other words, is there any cardinality between \aleph_0 and 2^{\aleph_0} ? This very famous conjecture became known as the Continuum Hypothesis (CH). In 1938, Kurt Gödel proved that this hypothesis is consistent with ZFC, which is the same thing as saying that there’s a model of ZFC – A “universe of sets” – in which CH is true. Some people believed this was an indication that CH is, indeed, true, which means that there are no models of ZFC in which CH is false. In fact, people generally had no idea how to build models of ZFC other than the “natural” ones like L which is the model built by Gödel. But Paul Cohen succeeded in doing just that, inventing the fundamental technique of Forcing in 1963. For this he was awarded the Fields medal. People don’t usually think of a model of ZFC+ \neg CH is a “counterexample”, but formally it can be regarded as one: it is a counterexample to the claim that ZFC implies CH, namely that there are no models of ZFC where CH is false. There are, in fact, such models, so Cohen built what might be described as a counterexample. Claim : An uncountable group must have an uncountable proper subgroup . (False!) It’s very easy to construct uncountable groups: the circle, the torus, the group of n\times n real matrices of determinant 1, and so on. There are tons of such groups, and if you look at them, you’ll see that they all insist on containing uncountable subgroups. Is it possible to create an uncountable group without uncountable proper subgroups? It’s possible, but very far from easy. The first counterexample, dubbed a “Kuroš monster”, was found by Saharon Shelah and published here . It’s beyond my abilities to even sketch the construction. Claim : There are no books dedicated exclusively to counterexamples . (False!) Topology has so many counterexamples, there’s a whole book about them, and this book is so famous, there’s a Wikipedia article about it. Following its success, other books with similar titles popped up in other fields of mathematics. Some of the standard counterexamples in topology are the Cantor set , the long line and the Hawaiian earring . A slightly more exotic counterexample is the “ Sticky foot ” space constructed by Bing as an example of a countable, connected Hausdorff space. It’s easy to suppose that a connected Hausdorff space must be uncountable, because all the connected spaces everyone knows are uncountable, and clearly the finite ones won’t do. But such weird spaces do exist, and the Sticky Foot space is one of them. Claim : This list is complete . (False!) This claim is nonsense. There are tons of other counterexamples in math, each of which serves as a counterexample to that claim.

How do you solve the functional equation f(f(x)f(y))+f(x+y)=f(xy)? (P2 from 2017 International Math Olympiad) — Let me take this opportunity to solve another math problem terribly . Problem 2 in the 2017 IMO was this functional equation: Problem 2 . Let \mathbb{R} be the set of real numbers. Determine all functions f:\mathbb{R} 	o \mathbb{R} such that, for all real numbers x and y , \displaystyle f(f(x)f(y)) + f(x + y) = f(xy) 	ag 1 The solution below is my own, and as per the SMPT philosophy, I’m presenting it along with my thought processes and multiple failures. A compact, clean solution can be written down in half a page. As with any functional equation, one of the first things you do is plug in some concrete values of the variables and see what happens. I started with x=y=0 which yields f(f(0)^2) + f(0) = f(0) f(f(0)^2) = 0 This doesn’t seem very helpful per se, but it does say that some number is taken by f to 0 . This is always a useful thing to know: 0 is in the image of f . I also noticed that this worked because f(x+y) and f(xy) were the same thing when x=y=0 , simply because x+y and xy are the same thing when x=y=0 . But x+y and xy are the same thing in many other cases, too. When? Well, given any value of x , we may wonder which value of y makes x+y=xy . Looking at x+y=xy as an equation in y , it is solved by y= rac{x}{x-1} . Oh, interesting: x=1 does not have a partner y which makes x+y=xy (because nothing makes 1+y=1\cdot y true), but any other x does. So there seem to be “lots of things” that are mapped to 0 by f : For any x
eq 1 , \displaystyle f\left(f(x)f\left( rac{x}{x-1}ight)ight) = 0 	ag 2 Of course at this point we still don’t know how many different values can f(x)f(x/(x-1)) obtain, but we do know that all of those values are mapped to 0 by f . Ok. That little detour actually saved us some work with checking special values for x and y ; for example, x=y=2 is already covered (because 2+2=2\cdot 2 , we know that f(f(2)^2)=0 , too). Trying other specific values, like x=1,y=2 , didn’t seem to be very illuminating. I next wondered what f(0) might be, since this is also a common stage in analyzing functional equations. Could it be that f(0)=0 ? Let’s assume that’s true, and check the original equation (1) with y=0 . We get, for every x , f(f(x)f(0))+f(x)=f(0) But if f(0)=0 then this says f(x) \equiv 0 , meaning f is just the zero function. Does it solve our functional equation? It sure does, so we have one possible (sort of degenerate) solution. This isn’t rare for functional equations, and so we set this aside and move on – but now we know that, if there are any other solutions to our equation, they must all satisfy f(0) 
eq 0 . I then looked at equation (2) again, which as you recall works for any x except 1 . What happens if x is such that f(x)=0 ? Then (2) becomes f(0) = 0 , which we now know isn’t true. Therefore f(x) cannot be 0 for any x . But wait… the first thing we discovered was that 0 is in the image of f . This apparent contradiction would have meant that we’re done – there aren’t any other solutions. But it doesn’t, since (2) excludes the value x=1 . Since there is some number which goes to 0 , and no number except x=1 may go to 0 , we have proven that f(1)=0 , and moreover, f(x)
