eq 1 . Nice: we’ve identified exactly who gets mapped to 0 . We observe that equation (2) says that f(	ext{something})=0 , which means that “something” must be 1 . So, for any x 
eq 1 , \displaystyle f(x)f\left( rac{x}{x-1}ight)=1 . That’s an interesting functional equation in its own right. It should be an instinct to explore the dynamics of the map x \mapsto x/(x-1) , in order to understand just how much rigidity this equation imposes on f . It turns out to be very little: applying this map twice yields the identity map, so really what this says is that half the numbers can do whatever they want and the other half is then determined, having the reciprocal value. This doesn’t turn out to be important, but it’s a natural exploration for anyone at this point. At this point I recalled that f(f(0)^2)=0 , which was the first thing we’ve found. So now we know that f(0)^2=1 , so f(0) = \pm 1 . This still leaves two options for f(0) , which cost me a lot of time going forward: I kept wondering which option I should pursue first, with the belief that once I’m done with it, the other would be similar. A better person than I would simply observe immediately that -f is a solution whenever f is, so of course f(0) is going to have two legitimate values if it has any (except 0 ), and we can just pick f(0)=1 for convenience and remember to add -f as another solution in the end. There are now two interesting things we can do with (1): we can see what happens when y=1 , and what happens when y=0 , since those are two cases where we already know f(y) . When y=1 we get \displaystyle f(f(x)f(1))+f(x+1)=f(x) \displaystyle f(0)+f(x+1)=f(x) \displaystyle 1+f(x+1)=f(x) \displaystyle f(x+1) = f(x)-1 	ag 3 that’s a nice relationship between the values of f at each point and the one +1 away. Of course it can also be run backwards: \displaystyle f(x-1) = f(x)+1 you get this just by replacing x with x-1 in (3) and rearranging. In particular, since f(0)=1 , we can conclude that f(n)=1-n for every natural number n . At this point you may guess, correctly, that f(x)=1-x is the solution we’re after (and f(x)=x-1 is the other). It’s easy to check that both of these solutions actually work, and we expect that those are the only ones. Our job, of course, is to prove this. Going back to (1) now with y=0 we get \displaystyle f(f(x))+f(x)=1 \displaystyle f(f(x)) = 1-f(x) 	ag 4 This is interesting. It almost says what we want. It says that if w happens to be f(x) for some x , then f(w)=1-w . In other words, f acts the way we expect on its own image – but we don’t know if its own image is everything. If we manage to prove that f is onto , then we’re done. This turned out to be easier to want to do than to do. To show that f is onto, you want to pick an arbitrary real number z and manipulate the equations until you find f(	ext{blah})=z , or even f(	ext{blah})=1-z or -z or 1/z or anything else that covers, or almost covers, all the real numbers. But our functional equation is all f 's! There are no free-standing expressions that aren’t wrapped as an argument of some f . This made the task of proving surjectivity beyond my powers, and unfortunately it took my quite a while to realize that it’s beyond my powers. At some point I went back to (4) and wondered what happens if I apply f to both sides. No, actually, that’s not what happened: I remembered that once you have f(f(x)) under control, it’s sometimes useful to evaluate f(f(f(x))) in two ways: one by thinking of it as f of f(f(x)) , and one by thinking of it as f(f) of f(x) . Using (4), this gives the two equations: f(f(f(x))) = f(1-f(x)) f(f(f(x))) = 1-f(f(x))=1-(1-f(x))=f(x) So those things are the same, which means that \displaystyle f(x) = f(1-f(x)) 	ag 5 This is crazy. We believe that f(x)=1-x must be true, and this equation is consistent with that, but once again it doesn’t quite imply it. In fact, if we knew that f was one-to-one (injective), then we could immediately conclude that x=1-f(x) , because for a one-to-one function, if f(	ext{foo})=f(	ext{bar}) then foo = bar. And this is crazy because we now have two paths to complete the proof: either prove that f is surjective, or prove that it is injective! Aargh! I spent forever jumping between these two paths. No progress on either. I was ready to give up. IMO contestants are now too smart for me. I used to solve IMO functional equations without much trouble. This one’s too hard! Here’s where I got stuck. To show that f is injective we need to pick two arbitrary real numbers a and b , assume that f(a)=f(b) , and conclude that a=b . Plugging a,b as is into (1) doesn’t seem to help at all, but I did quickly realize that what I really want is to find x,y so that x+y=a and xy=b . Why? Well because that forces f(x+y) and f(xy) to be the same, which is what served us so well in the beginning. But I was facing two problems. The smaller issue was that you can’t always find x,y whose sum is a and whose product is b . You have to have some discriminant come out positive for that to work. I wasn’t too worried about this, because I remembered equation (3): it lets you hop over by 1’s to the right or left quite freely, so I assumed that if need be I’ll just shift a,b to an appropriate location and all will be well. That, by the way, is indeed a good strategy, as we’ll see. The bigger issue was this: suppose I succeeded in finding x,y like that. Plugging them into (1) yields f(f(x)f(y)) = 0 so f(x)f(y)=1 . But here’s the problem: we know that f(x)f(y) is indeed 1 when y= rac{x}{x-1} , but we don’t know the reverse. We can’t conclude, from f(x)f(y)=1 , that y must be  rac{x}{x-1} . This is the same darn injectivity that we don’t have, because it is just what we’re trying to prove . Things would have been better if we had f(f(x)f(y)+1)=0 because then we could conclude that f(x)f(y)=0 , which says that f(x)=0 or f(y)=0 , meaning x=1 or y=1 . This is a nice, concrete conclusion to draw about x and y themselves, rather than their images under f . But how would we get this +1 in there? The answer, it finally occurred to me, is to use (3), and modify the definition of x,y . Instead of asking for x+y=a , xy=b , we are going to require x+y=a , xy=b-1 . Remember: a,b are just two numbers with f(a)=f(b) . We are defining x,y as solutions of x+y=a , xy=b-1 , which we may do because if we can’t, we will replace a,b by a-1,b-1 and keep doing so until b-1 is a negative number, at which point the equations x+y=a , xy=b-1 can be solved for real values of x,y . This “replace” step is fine because f(a)=f(b) if and only if f(a-1)=f(b-1) , thanks to (3). Ok. So now we have those x,y , and so \displaystyle f(f(x)f(y))+f(a) = f(b-1) \displaystyle f(f(x)f(y))+f(a) = f(b) + 1 \displaystyle f(f(x)f(y)) - 1 + f(a) = f(b) \displaystyle f(f(x)f(y)) - 1 = 0 \displaystyle f(f(x)f(y) + 1) = 0 This is just what we wanted. We conclude that x=1 or y=1 , and by symmetry it doesn’t matter which. Suppose y=1 . Then x+1=a , x=b-1 , meaning a=b which is (miracle of miracles!) just what we wanted. This is so stunningly pretty and unexpected, I’ve no idea how the person who came up with this problem came up with this problem. So, to wrap up: we somehow managed to show that f must be injective, which thanks to (5) means that f(x)=1-x . This was all under the assumption that f(0)=1 ; the case f(0)=-1 implies that -f satisfies -f(0)=1 , so then -f=1-x and so f=x-1 . Overall, we have proven that there are precisely three functions satisfying equation (1): f(x)=0 f(x)=1-x f(x)=x-1 And this is it. QED, but I’d never have gotten this on time in an actual IMO setting.
why-do-computers-take-more-time-in-prime: Why do computers take more time in prime factorization than in multiplication? The time difference is too much. — How long would it take you to mix a cup of sugar and a cup of salt? How long would it take you to separate them back? Many actions, even reversible ones, require very different resources to do and to undo. Multiplication is very much like fusing things together: we take the digits of the given numbers and perform a straightforward but intricate dance of shifting and mixing and adding, and the result is a tangled jumble of the original ingredients. Separating it back is, as far as we know and expect, as hard as unmixing flour and powdered sugar, particle by fine particle.
what-are-x-y-and-z-in-x-3-y-3-z-3-33: What are x, y, and z in x^3+y^3+z^3=33? — It depends. If you want three real numbers x,y,z satisfying x^3+y^3+z^3=33 then there are infinitely many, and they are very easy to find. If you want three rational numbers x,y,z satisfying x^3+y^3+z^3=33 then there are still infinitely many, though they are somewhat harder to find. If you want three integers , or whole numbers , satisfying that equation, then you'll need to be patient: nobody knows if such three numbers exist. 33 is the smallest natural number for which it is unknown if it can be represented as a sum of three cubes of integers. UPDATE (March 2019): This was just solved!! Andrew Booker [1] just discovered how to represent 33 as a sum of three integer cubes: \displaystyle \begin{aligned} a &= 8866128975287528 \\ b &= -8778405442862239 \\ c &= -2736111468807040 \\ 33 &= a^3+b^3+c^3\end{aligned} For real solutions, consider x=0, y=0, z=\sqrt[3]{33} or x=y=z=\sqrt[3]{11} or x=2, y=3, z=-\sqrt[3]{2} . There clearly are infinitely many solutions: you can choose x and y to be whatever you want, and there's always exactly one z that works, since every real number has exactly one real cube root. Want rational solutions? Here's a simple one: \displaystyle (-4)^3+\left(-\frac{5}{3}\right)^3+\left(\frac{14}{3}\right)^3=33 . Once again, there are infinitely many such solutions, though that's not quite as obvious as the real case. If you pick x and y to be rational, there's generally no reason to assume that the corresponding z will be rational as well – see the earlier examples of real solutions. But in fact, there are infinitely many ways of representing any rational number as the sum of three cubes of rationals. This was first discovered in 1825 by a schoolmaster from Leeds named S. Ryley, who published this discovery in “The Ladies’ Diary”, a publication which ran annually in London from 1704 to 1841, carrying the subtitle "Containing New Improvements in ARTS and SCIENCES, and many entertaining PARTICULARS: Designed for the USE AND DIVERSION OF THE FAIR SEX." One misses a time when the ladies of London were diverted by rational parametrizations of cubic equations. The problem of representing integers as sums of cubes of integers is very difficult. By simple considerations of residues modulo 9 , there are no such representations for numbers which leave a remainder of 4 or 5 upon division by 9 . For all other numbers, it is believed that such representations exist, but they are chaotic in a rather… diverting manner. 1=1^3+0^3+0^3 2=1^3+1^3+0^3 3=1^3+1^3+1^3 4 is ruled out 5 is ruled out 6=2^3+(-1)^3+(-1)^3 7=2^3+(-1)^3+0^3 8=2^3+0^3+0^3 9=2^3+1^3+0^3 10=2^3+1^3+1^3 11=3^3+(-2)^3+(-2)^3 12=10^3+7^3+(-11)^3 13 is ruled out 14 is ruled out 15=2^3+2^3+(-1)^3 16=2^3+2^3+0^3 17=2^3+2^3+1^3 18=3^3+(-2)^3+(-1)^3 19=3^3+(-2)^3+0^3 20=3^3+(-2)^3+1^3 21=16^3+(-14)^3+(-11)^3 22 is ruled out 23 is ruled out 24=2^3+2^3+2^3 25=3^3+(-1)^3+(-1)^3 26=3^3+(-1)^3+0^3 27=3^3+0^3+0^3 28=3^3+1^3+0^3 29=3^3+1^3+1^3 30=(-283059965)^3+(-2218888517)^3+2220422932^3 31 is ruled out 32 is ruled out 33 =??? Nobody knows . (EDIT: See above – now solved!) 34=3^3+2^3+(-1)^3 35=3^3+2^3+0^3 36=3^3+2^3+1^3 37=4^3+(-3)^3+0^3 38=4^3+(-3)^3+1^3 39=134476^3+117367^3+(-159380)^3 40 is ruled out 41 is ruled out 42= ??? Nobody knows . (EDIT: in Sep 2019, this was solved as well!) The solutions given here are the smallest possible. The representation of 39 was found in 1992 by Heath-Brown, Lioen and te Riele. The representation of 30 was found in 1999 by Beck, Pine, Tarrant and Yarbrough Jensen [2] . It is possible that some number not ruled out by the congruence condition has no such representation, though I feel it's unlikely. It is also possible that the numbers involved are beyond reach with present or even future technologies. Such is math: there are no guarantees. Footnotes [1] https://people.maths.bris.ac.uk/... [2] Mathematics of Computation
what-are-some-mathematical-proofs-which-: What are some mathematical proofs which appear to be correct, but are actually incorrect? — The most fiendish false proofs are not proofs of incorrect assertions. They are faulty proofs of correct assertions . When someone offers a proof of an incorrect assertion, you know that at some point in their chain of reasoning they must say something that’s wrong. Find that something, and you’ll see immediately where the proof fails. But when someone “proves”, incorrectly, a correct statement, demonstrating the incorrectness of the proof can be anywhere from easy to extremely hard. The assertions made in the steps of the proof may, for all we know, all be correct: it’s the implications that are broken. When students learn the idea of proofs, this is a point well worth emphasizing, and one of the tools is the study of incorrect proofs. It’s not used often enough, and that’s a shame. There’s much to be learned. Here are some of the best examples I know. The first example is a faulty proof by none other than Srinivasa Ramanujan . Now, granted, rigor in proofs was never Ramanujan’s forte; his breakthroughs were almost universally discoveries and conjectures, not proofs, which were supplied by others (sometimes decades after his death). But it’s interesting to study this case because this proof, or variations of it, still show up all the time. In 1911, Ramanujan published the following problem in the Journal of the Indian Mathematical Society : Evaluate the nested radicals \displaystyle \sqrt{1+2\sqrt{1+3\sqrt{1+4\sqrt{\cdots}}}} \displaystyle \sqrt{6+2\sqrt{7+3\sqrt{8+4\sqrt{\cdots}}}} The practice of publishing problems and asking for solutions by readers is still common, and when no solutions are offered the proposer is often expected to submit their own. Ramanujan published 58 such problems between 1911 and 1919, many of which are deep and fascinating. A wonderful survey of these problems is in this paper [1] by Berndt, Choi and Kang. Ramanujan’s own solution of these nested radicals runs as follows (we’ll do the first one; the other one is similar). Observe that \displaystyle n+2 = \sqrt{1+(n+1)(n+3)} Consequently, if we define f(n)=n(n+2) then \displaystyle f(n) = n\sqrt{1+f(n+1)} but then the same formula can be applied to the inner f(n+1) , yielding \displaystyle f(n) = n\sqrt{1+(n+1)\sqrt{1+f(n+2)}} and this can be repeated indefinitely, yielding an infinite nested radical. Finally, setting n=1 yields \displaystyle f(1) = \sqrt{1+2\sqrt{1+3\sqrt{\cdots}}} which is the desired nested radical, and of course f(1)=3 , so the answer is 3 . This seems both clever and convincing, but it’s incorrect – or at least, incomplete. Here’s the problem: we’ve managed to find one particular expression which, when repeatedly expanded, yields a sequence of nested radicals which approaches the desired one. But what if someone finds some other particular expression which also produces the same infinite nested radical, but with a different value? Indeed, this can actually be done. For example: 4 = \sqrt{1+2(15/2)} = \sqrt{1+2\sqrt{1+3(221/12)}}=\ldots this can also be pushed further indefinitely, and it seems to say that the value of the same nested radical is 4 ! (I stole this example from Herschfeld’s paper “On Infinite Radicals [2] ”). Which is it then? The situation may remind you of similar traps which come up with other infinite expressions. For example, when evaluating \displaystyle x = \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}^\cdots}} people often say that clearly x = \sqrt{2}^x , and this is satisfied by x=2 so the answer is 2 . But the problem is that x=\sqrt{2}^x is also satisfied by x=4 , so which is it? Part of the problem, of course, is that we need to carefully define what those infinite expressions even mean . This is typically done by declaring them to be limits of finite prefixes of themselves. Then, to evaluate them, we need to first prove that the limit exists, and then determine its value. Sometimes pinpointing the value can be done by studying fixed points of the iteration, as is the case with the infinite tower of \sqrt{2} 's. Ramanujan’s radical is more subtle since the iteration keeps changing. A complete and correct proof that the value is indeed 3 can be found in Herschfeld’s paper, and I think there’s also a question about this on Quora. The Cayley-Hamilton theorem (in its matrix formulation) states that if A is a square matrix (over some field) and p_A(t)=\det(A-It) is its characteristic polynomial then p_A(A)=0 . This is not a terribly difficult theorem, but it’s not quite straightforward either. Most courses on linear algebra present one of the correct proofs, and the students move on. However, few teachers pause to show the following incorrect argument: we want to show that p_A(A)=0 . Well, what’s p_A(t) ? Why, it is \det(A-It) where I is the identity matrix of the appropriate size. Ok, so what’s p_A(A) ? Obviously, it is \det(A-IA) = \det(A-A)=0 . Done, QED. Here’s the thing: if any teacher actually walked their class through this “argument”, with a poker face and a confident attitude, I guarantee you nobody would raise their hand to protest. It seems clear, easy, obvious and straightforward. Doesn’t it? And furthermore, what it proves is actually true, so nobody can find a counterexample. This is most definitely a proof which “appears to be correct”. It’s a really good exercise to ponder this “argument” and see why it fails. There’s actually a relatively easy howler here, created by our poor notation. Ask yourself, what is “ 0 "? Wait, what do you mean “what is 0 "? Seems like a silly question. Well, look again at the statement p_A(A)=0 . A careful teacher would write p_A(A) = \mathbf{0} , a bold zero denoting the zero matrix . Indeed, what the Cayley-Hamilton theorem says it that if you calculate c_0I+c_1A+c_2A^2+\ldots+c_nA^n where c_i are the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial, then you get the zero matrix . You get a matrix, not a number. On the other hand, our “proof” ended with \det(A-A)=0 , the number zero. The number zero is not the matrix zero. Our “proof”, whatever it shows, only concludes that a certain number is zero. This isn’t what the theorem says. Whenever I teach the C-H theorem to anyone I make a point of showing this silly non-proof. It’s actually not silly. It stresses the meaning of the theorem and lets students see how misleading proofs can be if we don’t pay careful attention. Famously, in 1879, Alfred Kempe published a proof of the 4-color theorem using the (very clever) idea of flipping colors along what are now known as Kempe Chains. The proof stood and was accepted for 11 years before Heawood found a critical error, in 1890. Briefly, the proof runs as follows. Assume that the 4-color-theorem is false, and pick a minimal counterexample: a planar graph which is not 4-colorable. We may assume that the graph is that of a triangulation, and using Euler’s formula we show that the graph must contain a vertex v of degree \le 5. If we remove vertex v (and its incident edges), the leftover graph can be colored with 4 colors, since we picked a minimal counterexample. Our goal is to show that we can still use just 4 colors even if we put that vertex back. If v has degree 3 or less, that’s obvious: at worst, three colors are unavailable for our vertex, so we can use a fourth one. If v has degree 4, we may assume that the coloring of the leftover graph uses all four colors for its neighbors, let’s say Blue, Red, Green and Yellow as you walk around the vertex. Put yourself at the Blue vertex and attempt to walk all the way to the Green one only using Blue/Green vertices. Either you can or you can’t. If you can’t, good news: flip all the colors along your walk from Blue to Green. Now our vertex sees only Red, Yellow and two Greens, so it can be colored Blue. If you can complete the walk, the flipping doesn’t help, of course, because the Green became Blue but the Blue became Green. But now repeat the argument with the Red-Yellow vertices. It’s impossible for two closed loops to form, one Blue-Green and the other Red-Yellow, because planar graphs can’t have two such non-intersecting loops. This proves the reduction for the degree-4 case. Everything up to this point is perfectly valid . Kempe then moved on to repeat the argument for degree 5, which is where he subtly tripped up. He considered a coloring around v going R-B-R-G-Y, and worked with similar chains as before. If both the R vertices are surrounded by blocking chains, he attempted to create a R-G chain and a R-Y chain and simultaneously flip them; but this can’t work because the flips may clash with each other. The error is subtle, but the proof is unfixable. It took over 80 years to produce a correct proof of 4CT, relying on extensive computer calculations. The basic logical structure of the proof can be traced back to Kempe’s original idea: we work with minimal counterexamples and “unavoidable configurations”, which for Kempe were simply vertices of degree at most 5, and we show that they can be “reduced”, meaning they can always be recolored with fewer colors. But the details of the eventual proof were much more complicated than Kempe believed. Finally, let’s recall that “proofs which appear to be correct” can be extremely serious and difficult affairs. In 1993, Andrew Wiles had a proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem which he was completely confident in. He is a very, very careful mathematician, and quite shy; “coming out” with such a sensational proof was a difficult step, but he did it because he knew he had it. He presented the proof in a series of lectures, and submitted a full write-up for publication. Nick Katz [3] began the monumental task of reviewing Wiles’ paper. Few people were even capable of doing that, but Katz had both the immense knowledge and the meticulous nature required to comprehend and check everything very, very carefully. He wrote to Wiles whenever something was unclear, and Wiles always responded with clarifications. Until that one time when he couldn’t. They discussed the point back and forth over weeks, and it became clear that there was a problem, and it was not a trifle, and then it became deep, and then it became an irreversible flaw that demolished the entire proof. It wasn’t even directly something in Wiles’ proof, as far as my understanding goes: it was an issue with a construction by Flach [4] , then a young researcher, now himself a renowned mathematician at Caltech (we should hold none of that against him – these things happen). Wiles had to go back to the proverbial drawing board, now under immense pressure knowing that his edifice is out and the whole world is chasing the elusive proof. It was a terrible time. Eventually, he made a dramatic breakthrough: the very thing that blocked Flach’s construction from working turned out to resurrect a completely different approach to the proof which Wiles abandoned years earlier. He rebuilt the whole thing, recruiting Richard Taylor for a difficult ring-theoretic argument, and successfully published a complete and correct proof in 1995. His 1993 proof certainly “appeared to be correct” to his audience and the first round of readers, and most of all, to himself. It was incorrect, but from its ashes emerged the correct proof, one of the greatest mathematical breakthroughs of the 20th century. Footnotes [1] The Problems Submitted by Ramanujan to the Journal of the Indian Mathematical Society [2] https://www.jstor.org/stable/230... [3] Nick Katz - Wikipedia [4] Matthias Flach (mathematician) - Wikipedia
why-did-riemann-propose-the-riemann-zeta: Why did Riemann propose the Riemann zeta function? — Riemann was, first and foremost, a geometer. His deep research into the structure and geometry of manifolds set the stage for the field known today as Riemannian Geometry, which is fundamental for many domains of math and physics. Riemann wrote a single paper on number theory. One. That paper, the 1859 "On the number of primes less than a given magnitude", was ten (10) pages long, and it spawned a whole new field that is being intensely researched to this day. He wrote it at the suggestion of Gauss, who somehow felt that the young prodigy could do something meaningful in that domain. Riemann's unbelievably deep insight was that he can take a fairly simple-looking function defined by Euler, apply the very new idea of analytic continuation to extend that function into areas where it didn't previously exist, perform Fourier inversion on the result, and obtain a profound new formula for the number of primes less than a given value. That was his main goal: to study the frequency at which prime numbers show up. The hypothesis known today as the Prime Number Theorem, which says that there are about x/\log(x) primes up to x , was already in the air - Gauss guessed it and others (mostly Chebyshev) had started making progress towards it. Riemann had a brilliant idea for attacking such questions using the tools of complex function theory and Fourier methods, and this idea centered on the function that today bears his name. The basic connection between the function \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^s} and prime numbers was already observed by Euler, decades earlier. But pushing this fairly simple observation into a profound theory required Riemann's ingenious plan. Every step of this plan was new and technically demanding. The whole program was shockingly original, and this was likely one of the single most important breakthroughs in the history of mathematics. Ten pages. You can read the whole thing (in English+math) here .
how-would-i-go-about-getting-a-math-phd-: How would I go about getting a math PhD by the age of 25? — I have the will and the passion to want to get such a thing. I love math beyond all things. Being only 14, I (surprisingly) have found my passion and I know that a math PhD is my goal. I’ve begun studying Linear Algebra and finished up with Multivariable Calculus in about a month. My dreams are set. You have found your passion, and it is math. Your dreams are set. That's awesome (no, really. It is). Here's my advice, if you care to hear it: learn to play a musical instrument . I don't mean that you shouldn't dedicate time to learning math. You should, and we’ll get to that. But given your drive, this isn't what you need to worry about. That'll happen. You do need to worry about not making your teenage years be about just this one thing. When you grow up, several things may happen, some more likely than others. You may find that you have other interests, including things you never even tried, or knew existed. You may feel an urge to start a family, and you may need to learn to maneuver socially and romantically. You may feel burnt out by math. You may need to make a living and a suitable academic position may be unavailable. Who knows. At 14, you may feel your life can be planned. It almost certainly cannot. Your job is to do the best you can to set yourself up for a fulfilling, happy life. Focusing on your passion is a good thing, but betting everything on a single outcome is almost certainly folly. There's more to life than math, and I say that as someone whose whole life is structured with math at its very core. There's no particular need to earn a Ph.D. by age 25, specifically. You have a long life ahead of you. Don't optimize for speed. Earning a graduate degree by that time doesn't really force you to do anything crazy right now – you can comfortably finish you undergrad by 21 and complete a thesis in four years, it’s fine – but it doesn't matter. Maybe you'll already be married. Maybe you'll have had a job or two. Maybe you'll get your Ph.D. at 29 and find a position at a great university. Don't worry about achieving X by age Y. Worry about learning, developing kindness and discipline, broadening your horizons, and (when you're ready), dating. I'm not kidding. I've seen teenagers spend years with math and little else, and there's a heavy price to pay. Learning to play a musical instrument is a really good way to make progress along some of the non-math dimensions I've mentioned. It's not the only way, of course, but it's a really good one. Do it. Also, read books. Prose. Poetry. Study physics, and programming, and world history. Travel, if you can. Hike, bike or do some sport, any sport. Now, as for the math itself: I don't know where you live and what resources you have available, but it'll be useful to find learning environments that emphasize math to some extent. Take advanced classes if you can. Take courses at a college nearby during high school, if you can. If at all possible find a tutor, a group of people to study with, a guide, a mentor. It's a wonderful journey but it's not easy to do it alone. Make sure you spend time solving problems and proving things. Have someone knowledgeable review your proofs. Don't rely on your own feedback. Read books, and do the exercises . Reading alone is meaningless. Don't read the solutions unless you're really, totally and absolutely stuck, and if you are, ask for a hint first. Knowing nothing else about you this is about as specific as I can get. Follow your dream and have fun, just don't forget to live while you're at it.
how-can-i-solve-an-equation-of-the-third: How can I solve an equation of the third degree? — There is more than one way to interpret "solve" in the context of equations in general, and polynomial equations in particular. In practice, most often you would solve a cubic equation (3rd degree) by guessing one solution x_1 , dividing the cubic by x-x_1 and then solving the resulting quadratic equation (2nd degree) as usual. You can also solve any such equation numerically, for example using Newton's method . However, when people talk about "solving an equation of the 3rd degree", they usually mean a solution by radicals . This means a way to write the three solutions as expressions involving the coefficients of the original equation, square roots, cubic roots, and arithmetic operations. The quadratic formula x_{1,2} = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a} is, famously, a way to express the roots of the quadratic equation ax^2+bx+c=0 in this way. Why should anyone care? Honestly, cubic equations aren't that important. They do occur here and there "in real life" and in abstract math, but they're not really fundamentally vital. However, the method of solution has tremendous historical importance and considerable beauty, and therein lies its real value . It's amazing that mankind attempted to solve cubic equations for thousands of years, eventually succeeding after the dedicated efforts of countless people, yet so few today - even those with considerable mathematical training - are able to remember the algorithm well enough to be able to use it or explain it on demand, without looking it up. This was one of the key intellectual achievements of the renaissance, a significant breakaway from the frontiers of classical knowledge, and I think it deserves to be better known. It's not really that difficult, anyway. Ready? The Classical Approach We're trying to solve an equation that looks like ax^3+bx^2+cx+d=0 where the coefficients a,b,c,d are some numbers. In fact, I'm going to focus on what seems like a very special case: (1) x^3 + cx + d = 0 . The reason for this focus is that reducing a general cubic to this form is fairly straightforward, so I'll leave this to the end. The real gem is this special case. You can play around with this equation for days and months to no avail - the algebraic manipulations we know and love just don't do anything here. The crucial idea is to perform a daring gambit, replacing the single unknown x with a sum of two unknowns p, q . So we just boldly write x=p+q . How can this be a good thing? We need to determine one number x , and now we have two unknowns to deal with? Well, sure, but we also have a new degree of freedom - we can impose another condition on p and q while allowing them to still add up to x . Maybe that'll save us (hint: it does). This is the only part of the solution that you need to pull out of a hat . The rest is algebra. Let's put that p+q in our equation to be solved (1). We get (p+q)^3 + c(p+q) + d = 0 Expanding the cube, this is p^3 + q^3 + 3p^2q + 3pq^2 + c(p+q) + d = 0 . We leave the cubes alone but observe that there's another p+q hiding in the mixed terms: p^3 + q^3 + 3pq(p+q) + c(p+q) + d = 0 . We see a repeated term p+q , so we naturally collect the terms that contain it: p^3 + q^3 + (3pq+c)(p+q) + d = 0 . Now comes the kicker: remember that extra degree of freedom we have? We can use it to eliminate this whole mess in the middle. Quite simply, we nonchalantly impose that 3pq+c is to vanish . 3pq+c = 0 Or: (2) q = -\frac{c}{3p} . Our equation is now: p^3 - \frac{c^3}{27p^3} + d = 0 . And we're done!! Wait. Why are we done? Well, if you've solved many high-school quadratic exercises, you may recognize that the last equation is merely a quadratic in disguise. There's only one variable now, and that is p . It only appears in the equation as p^3 , so we might as well call z = p^3 and get z - \frac{c^3}{27z} + d = 0 or z^2 + dz - \frac{c^3}{27}= 0 , A measly quadratic. Solve it, find the possible values of z , infer the possible values of p (including the complex ones!), determine q (remember equation (2)), and add them up to get x . TADAAA!!! A Worked Example Let's try to go through those steps with a concrete equation: x^3 - 7x + 6 = 0 . Once again, the way you really solve this is by guessing a solution (quite easy in this case), eliminating that solution and solving the quadratic. Takes about 2 minutes here. But no - we're going to follow the recipe. It's going to be way harder, introducing complex numbers along the way, but the beauty of it is that it's a recipe , requiring no guesses and guaranteed to work. Always. So, we make x=p+q , p^3+q^3+3p^2q+3pq^2 - 7(p+q) + 6 = 0 p^3 + q^3 + 3pq(p+q) - 7(p+q) + 6 = 0 p^3 + q^3 + (3pq-7)(p+q) + 6 = 0 We now declare that 3pq = 7 , or q = \frac{7}{3p} getting p^3 + \frac{343}{27p^3} + 6 = 0 or, letting z = p^3 , z + \frac{343}{27z} + 6 = 0 z^2 + 6z + \frac{343}{27} = 0 This is somewhat hairy, but we plow through and find z = -3 \pm \frac{10\sqrt{3}}{9}i . The next task is to find the p s which correspond to each of those z s. This is a matter of extracting cube roots of a complex number, a tricky but not insurmountable task. Let's find the cube roots of the one with the + sign (it turns out that this is enough - repeating the task for the other value will yield the same roots again). They are: p_1 = -\frac{3}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{6}i p_2 = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{5\sqrt{3}}{6} i p_3 = 1 + \frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3} i For each of these, we calculate q = 7/(3p) , add p+q and find the values of x , which turn out to be... x_1 = p_1 + \frac{7}{3p_1} = -3 x_2 = p_2 + \frac{7}{3p_2} = 1 x_3 = p_3 + \frac{7}{3p_3} = 2 . Well. The roots turned out to be fairly simple numbers: -3, 1 and 2. That certainly could have been guessed. The method is impressively inefficient in this particular case, forcing us to work with these complex expressions only to get such simple answers eventually. But again: this is foolproof recipe that works for any cubic equation of the form x^3+b x + c = 0 . The General Cubic So far we dealt with the special case x^3+bx+c=0 . In the general case, you start with ax^3+bx^2+cx+d = 0 . First, divide through by a to get rid of the leading coefficient (we assume that a \neq 0 , otherwise it's not a cubic). You now have something like this (renaming the variables to keep things simple): x^3+bx^2+cx+d = 0 . The coefficient b is minus the sum of the roots. This is just a special case of Vieta's formulas , but if you're not familiar with them you can easily see this by writing x^3+bx^2+cx+d = (x-x_1)(x-x_2)(x-x_3) , expanding and equating coefficients of x^2 . This means that if we shift x by b/3 , the sum of the roots of the new equation will be 0. Indeed, let y = x+b/3 or x = y-b/3 , substitute in the equation, and observe how x^3 contributes a factor of -by^2 and the bx^2 term contributes by^2 making the quadratic term disappear. This is much easier to do in specific instances than by following the formulas. If you don't remember what you need to shift the variable by, just write x = y - t , substitute and then find the value of t that makes the square term vanish. Once you're done solving the formula for y , which is now in the correct form, just remember to subtract b/3 from each solution to get the values of the original x . That's it!
have-you-created-a-problem-that-you-coul: Have you created a problem that you couldn't solve in math or logic but that someone else could? — That's actually one of my happiest achievements in mathematics. Some years ago I came up with a conjecture based on a combination of wishful thinking, minuscule amounts of data and extremely vague intuition. I made some progress on one half of my own conjecture but wasn't able to resolve it completely, and I had no idea how to tackle the other half. The conjecture apparently spread around and eventually both halves were solved and published by people I don't personally know at all. In some ways, this made me more proud than my own published results. I asked a good question! Background Given a finite group G and an expression such as XY^2Z^{-1}X^{-1}ZY^{-1} , one may ask about the values of the expression if random elements of G are substituted into the variables X,Y,Z . Officially, the "expression" is an element of the free group with some finite number of generators, and it's pretty natural to ask about what you get when you evaluate such words when group elements are assigned to the generators. Specifically, if you plug in uniform, random elements of a finite group into some such expression, what is the probability that you get 1 , the identity element? Is this probability at least some positive constant, perhaps depending on G but not on the expression? It is not so strange to guess that the identity should come up often when you evaluate such expressions. In fact, it's easy to see that this must be the case when the group is abelian, for example. It's also reasonable to assume that given that the expression is not allowed to contain any constants. The Conjecture After lots of experimentation, partial results, staring at pages full of calculations, false proofs and wrong turns, I proposed the following conjecture: A finite group G is solvable if and only if there exists some positive constant c>0 (depending on G ) such that, for every r \in \mathbb{N} and every w \in F_r (the free group on r generators), the probability that w(g_1,\ldots,g_r)=1 is at least c , where the g_i are uniformly, independently chosen elements of G . As promised, this conjecture has two halves: Showing that for solvable groups you can never contrive a word that pushes the probability down below some fixed positive constant (the probability of getting 1 is "bounded away from 0"). Showing that for non-solvable groups you can always come up with a sequence of contrived words that do push the probability as close to 0 as you wish. This conjecture seemed attractive to me for several reasons. First, it's quite elementary, requiring nothing more than the definition of a group (even the notion of a free group is not really needed here). Second, there's no obvious reason why "solvability" is the right dividing line here, and it's quite pleasing that it is: the condition of solvability originally came about from the relationship between groups and solvability of polynomials by radicals, and here we are re-interpreting it as "ease of solving equations inside the group". Indeed, the conjecture can be regarded as saying that equations like XY^2Z^{-1}X^{-1}ZY^{-1} = 1 are easy to solve in solvable groups and possibly hard to solve in non-solvable groups. Doesn't that sound quaint? The Resolution I made no explicit effort to publicize the conjecture. I never published it, nor my proof of the first half in the case that G is nilpotent. Somehow it made the rounds; some friends from grad school heard me discuss it and told their friends, my thesis advisor mentioned it to a few people, and eventually people smart enough to tackle it actually found it interesting enough to tackle, and solved it. It took about 4 years after the conjecture came into being. The second half was solved first, by Miklós Abért in 2005: On the probability of satisfying a word in a group . The first half was solved by Nikolay Nikolov and Dan Segal, who were thus able to state the result as A characterization of finite soluble groups , published in the Bulletin of the LMS in 2006. While looking up the links for this answer I noticed that more people are aware of those results and are finding them interesting (here's one example on Mathoverflow ). I can't quite describe how happy this makes me. EDIT: I just discovered that the first half became Problem 5 in the 2004 Miklós Schweitzer Competition!

how-did-germany-lose-its-edge-in-mathema: How did Germany lose its edge in mathematics? — Judging a country’s level of excellence in mathematics by the number of Fields medal recipients is dubious (and I’ll be shocked if Germany doesn’t land another Fields at the next ICM*), but it cannot be denied that Germany’s position among countries in mathematical research is no longer what it was at the beginning of the 20th century. Assigning cause and effect to such historical processes is often difficult, but in this case one key event can actually be pinpointed with reasonable reliability: the rise of the Nazis and the expulsion of Jewish scientists from German universities, particularly Göttingen, in the years leading to WWII. In 1934, David Hilbert was sitting next to the Nazis' newly appointed minister of education [ Bernhard Rust - AA ], at a banquet. When asked, "And how is mathematics in Göttingen, now that it has been freed of the Jewish influence?" Hilbert replied: "Mathematics in Göttingen? There is really no such thing any more." [1] The name “ Göttingen ” doesn’t mean much to most people nowadays, but mathematicians are well aware of the superstars who did their chief work there: Gauss, Riemann, Dirichlet, Hilbert, Klein, Noether, Weyl. Such a succession of luminaries did not occur, as far as I can tell, anywhere else before or after, and it was all set to continue this illustrious trajectory into the late 20th century. But during the 1930’s, Göttingen died. In 1933, the Nazis began to systematically drive Jewish mathematicians and scientists away from Germany. Among those directly affected were physicists Max Born , Leo Szilard , Edward Teller , Hans Bethe and another one whose name escapes me right now. Ah, yes: Albert Einstein . In mathematics, suffice it to mention the names of Edmund Landau , Emmy Noether , Felix Bernstein , Richard Brauer , Eugene Wigner , Felix Hausdorff , Hermann Weyl (whose wife was Jewish), Max Dehn (who survived a bit longer than the others, but eventually was forced to flee), Richard Courant , and of course, John von Neumann . For this man alone to move from one country to another could alter the course of history. Göttingen never regained anything close to its former prominence, and neither did Germany. Hasse and Siegel , two mathematical luminaries, tried to resurrect it, but failed. (Hasse was a right-wing nationalist, but he was denied a membership in the Nazi party because he actually had Jewish roots). And who knows, if not for the Nazis, Grothendieck himself may have remained a German. * Added later: I wrote that because I expected Peter Scholze to be a laureate in 2018, and indeed he was. Footnotes [1] Historical Encyclopedia of Natural and Mathematical Sciences
how-did-andrew-wiles-succeed-in-proving-: How did Andrew Wiles succeed in proving Fermat's last theorem when others had failed? — A facetious, provocative answer with a shred of truth: he did not . Andrew Wiles didn't actually prove Fermat's Last Theorem. Not directly. He proved a much deeper and more important result, the Modularity Theorem for Elliptic Curves (not all of it, but a huge and sufficiently big chunk). The guy who proved that FLT follows from the Modularity conjecture was Ken Ribet, building on work by Serre following the original ideas of Frey and Hellegouarch. But this happened chronologically earlier, so the credit for providing the final ingredient goes, justifiably, to Wiles. In a way, the question should be: how did Frey and Hellegouarch succeed in devising a new attack on FLT while others did not? Because really, the FLT-specific ingredient of this chain of events is theirs. The subsequent work (Serre, Ribet, Wiles) was much more broad and general, and was inspired and motivated by the original discovery that FLT, which seems to have nothing to do with elliptic curves and modular forms, can nevertheless be approached with these tools. So how did Frey and Hellegouarch manage to do this while others before them did not? First of all, let's not take away from the fact that their (independent) ideas were a fantastic spark of genius. But this spark doesn't exist in a vacuum. Mathematicians of the 18th and 19th and early 20th centuries couldn't possibly have devised this idea because the world wasn't ready: Frey and Hellegouarch lived at a time where we already knew a great deal about elliptic curves and their relationship with both number theory and automorphic forms. It still took genius, but this genius had a substrate to spring from. The Modularity conjecture was in the air. We knew that elliptic curves can't just do whatever the hell they want. Frey could dream up an elliptic curve from a purported solution of FLT and intuitively see that it must have weird properties, even though he couldn't prove that it truly can't be modular. Ribet did that. Why did Ribet succeed where others have not? Well, before Frey nobody was really motivated to prove that, and then Serre formulated the precise general conjecture that would imply that Frey's curve can't be modular, and few people in the world were better prepared to solve that conjecture than Ken Ribet. Once again, let's not diminish the fact that his achievement was pure genius (it was he, actually, who proved FLT! If the Modularity conjecture was already solved, that honor would fall to him). But Ribet's breakthrough didn't exist in a vacuum either. It was impossible for anyone to do what he did years or decades earlier; the foundations weren't there. Ribet's work left the Modularity conjecture to be solved. Wiles succeeded in doing that, together with Richard Taylor who helped him complete a crucial part. Why he? Because once again, he was uniquely positioned to. He already did profound work in this direction earlier in his career, and few people in the world knew more than he did about these concepts and ideas. But once again, this doesn't take away from the fact that his success required both enormous tenacity and tremendous ingenuity. He had a great starting position: the world's collective progress in the relevant theories, his own deep researches into them, and the huge motivation boost he got from Ribet's work. But even given all those existing conditions, his achievement is one of the most singular breakthroughs in the history of mathematics. He's just that good.
how-many-prime-numbers-in-total-are-know: How many prime numbers in total are known as of November 2020? — Let’s head over to Wolfram|Alpha together. Wolfram|Alpha Type in “Random 1000 digit prime”. Wait a few seconds. You should see something like this: You can tap “More digits” to see more digits. Eventually you can observe all 1000 of them. Congratulations! There is now one more known prime than there was a few seconds ago. And you are the only person who knows it! Wait. How can I know this? Well, strictly speaking, I can’t. It is possible that someone, somewhere, has hit upon that very prime you just discovered. But this is… shall we say, stupendously unlikely? There are more than 10^{996} primes with a thousand decimal digits. The entire visible universe cannot store more than, oh, 10^{70} of them, if I’m being very generous. That means that the chances that your personal prime is or was already observed are less than one in 10^{900} , which is googol to the ninth power. I wouldn’t try to express that number using trillions and quadrillions. It’s like winning the finest prize of your country’s lottery, and then winning it again, and again, and again, a hundred times in a row. So I think we can safely say that every time you or anyone else asks Wolfram|Alpha, or any other piece of software, for a random prime of decent size, there’s a new known prime. And this, as you may know, happens quite a few times per day, for various cryptographic reasons. And therefore, there’s no such thing as “the number of known primes as of November 2020”. This isn’t an actual magnitude of anything meaningful.
what-is-it-like-to-prove-a-theorem-no-on: What is it like to prove a theorem no one has ever proven before? — It’s a special, peculiar, lovely, lonely thrill. How big of a thrill depends on the circumstances. The theorem could be tiny or huge, famous or unknown, profound or superficial, nifty or stunning, a small improvement over the current state of the art or a complete breakthrough. Just how big of a thrill it can be I can’t tell you: I did not prove anything close to a famous conjecture. But I did get a chance to prove new things, some (I think) interesting and non-trivial. And it was awesome. Problem solving is great fun (for some of us), but there’s an extra level of satisfaction in solving something that no one solved before – even if perhaps no one even tried to solve it before, but of course even more so if people did. When you wrestle with a math olympiad or a Putnam problem, it’s like a game: you know that the problem was designed to have a solution. It takes creativity and cleverness and experience to find it, but everyone knows it’s there. But when you wrestle with a conjecture you came up with yourself, or your thesis advisor did, or something that is being investigated by others, then you don’t know if it is at all possible to prove it, or even if it’s true. It’s a mystery, and you feel like exploring a totally new domain: a place no one visited before you. Finding the final spark that makes everything work is a fantastically satisfying – and rare – pleasure. It may have taken two days, or six weeks, or a few years, and you may have given up on it, and it came back to haunt you, and you gave it more love, and then it paid back. I don’t know that there are great analogies to explain what it is “like”; perhaps it’s like reaching a summit, but rather than a deliberate expedition to attempt Nanga Parbat, it’s like walking for ages in empty deserts and dense jungles and suddenly finding a brand new peak, and negotiating it, and besting it. Really, I don’t think it’s like anything else. I wish I possessed the eloquence to describe it.
a-machine-outputs-random-real-numbers-be: A machine outputs random real numbers between 0 and 1, until their sum exceeds 1. How many numbers will it need to generate, on average? — Here's a little trick that's often useful: when a random variable takes on positive integer values, its expectation is The probability that it is at least 1, plus The probability that it is at least 2, plus The probability that it is at least 3, plus …and so on. The reason is simple: the probability that it is exactly 7 shows up 7 times in this infinite sum. So overall, this is just the sum of k times the probability of k , which is the expectation. Why is that useful? You see, when you’re working with a random variable such as “number of times until the sum exceeds 1”, or more generally a “stopping time” or “first success” kind of thing, the probability that it is exactly 7 is a little annoying to calculate: it’s the probability that you didn’t succeed in steps 1 through 6, but then did succeed in step 7. Instead, the probability that it is at least 7 is nothing more nor less than the probability that the first 6 steps failed. This is almost always a simpler expression. In our case, the chances that you need at least k+1 numbers for the sum to exceed 1 is just the probability that the first k numbers chosen add up to less than 1 . This is a simple volume calculation: The length of the segment 0\leq x\leq 1 is 1 . The area of the triangle x+y\leq 1 , with x,y\geq 0 , is 1/2 . The volume of the pyramid x+y+z\leq 1 , with x,y,z\geq 0 , is 1/6 . …and so on. The volume of the polyhedron x_1+\ldots x_k\leq 1 when x_1,\ldots x_k\geq 0 is 1/k! . Therefore, the expectation we are looking for is simply the sum of 1/k! over all k (including k=0 ), which is simply e .
how-do-i-prove-that-sqrt-n-sqrt-n-is-irr: How do I prove that \sqrt{n+\sqrt{n}} is irrational? — We are assuming, of course, that n is a positive integer. If \displaystyle x=\sqrt{n+\sqrt{n}} then \displaystyle x^2=n+\sqrt{n} \displaystyle x^2-n=\sqrt{n} \displaystyle (x^2-n)^2=n \displaystyle x^4-2nx^2+(n^2-n)=0 This is a monic polynomial (leading coefficient 1 ) with integer coefficients. Rational roots of such polynomials must actually be integers (proof: clear the denominators. This is sometimes called the “rational root theorem”). So we already know that if \sqrt{n+\sqrt{n}} wants to be rational then it must actually be an integer. Can it? If it is, then n+\sqrt{n} is also an integer, in fact a perfect square. But then \sqrt{n} is an integer, so n=m^2 for some m , and n+\sqrt{n}=m^2+m . This is not a perfect square: it sits strictly between m^2 and (m+1)^2=m^2+2m+1 . Therefore, \sqrt{n+\sqrt{n}} is not an integer, so it’s irrational. QED
